articles.title_orig: Oat of this world: cooks descend on Scotland for ultimate porridge making contest
articles.title_zh: Oat of this world: cooks descend on Scotland for ultimate porridge making contest
articles.content_orig:
Technical mishaps and plenty of whisky as competitors from as far afield as US and Australia vie for Golden Spurtle
T here are many varieties of spurtle. The traditional Scottish cooking implement, designed for stirring porridge without forming lumps, comes in a range of sizes, can be formed from cherry wood, beech, or maple, and might be topped with a decorative finial or smoothed out at its end for a more modern finish. But on Saturday in Carrbridge, in the Scottish Highlands, only one spurtle mattered: the Golden Spurtle, awarded annually to the winner of the World Porridge Making championship, which have been hosted here since 1994.
The sun shone on the picturesque village as almost 40 competitors lined up in the village hall for six heats across the day. Tasked with producing a traditional porridge – made only from untreated oatmeal, water and salt – and a speciality dish where additional ingredients and flourishes were permitted, entrants had travelled from across Scotland and as far afield as Australia and the US for a shot at the Golden Spurtle.
As the first heat kicked off, technical difficulties beset some contestants when the provided induction hobs, new this year after a long tradition of gas, failed to heat. But the reigning champion, Norway’s Sven Seljom, was unaffected, serenely stirring Norwegian mutton into oats and filtered water he had brought with him especially for the competition. He had planned to bring Norwegian cheese, too, he said, but import rules meant he had to make do with something more local. A sizeable entourage watched on in traditional Scandinavian dress as he measured, stirred and tasted, boisterous chants of “SVEN, SVEN, SVEN” breaking out at each mention of his name.
The first of the day’s many whisky breaks came 10 minutes into proceedings at 10.40am, with shots of a lowland malt distributed throughout the exuberant crowd as competitors did well to retain their focus. The drams’ effects meant nobody seemed to mind too much when the crucial timer was accidentally reset just moments from the heat’s tense final countdown.
Any initial teething problems were quickly ironed out as the day settled into a well-oiled rhythm. In a separate “judging chamber”, a trio of judges from Scotland’s culinary scene blind-tasted each batch, assessing primarily for taste, texture and colour. Among the speciality porridges on offer throughout the day were a “Granola Espanola”, a porridge cannoli from the Australian national champion, Robert Reid , and a recipe featuring soft-boiled quail eggs.
“The first thing I did was burn my oats,” lamented Switzerland’s Jeremy McTeague after a heat that didn’t quite go to plan. But he remained upbeat: “It gave them a distinctive toastiness – maybe the judges will like it.”
Hundreds of spectators showed up for the day’s spectacle, from Carrbridge residents who turn out each year to support the community-powered event, to tourists such as Joe, 43, and Tina, 39, who were visiting from England and had overheard a conversation about the championship in a local pub the previous night.
“We looked it up and decided straight away we’d be here,” said Joe. “It’s Scotland, it’s porridge, someone said there would be whisky … it was a no-brainer.” The pair said they were making a beeline for the tasting room to sample the produce left over from judging.
The event proved so popular that the village hall had to operate a one-in, one-out policy. Those who couldn’t fit inside were decanted into a merch tent bursting with oats, spurtles and “always stir clockwise” tote bags, while local cafes and tourist centres screened a live stream of the competition. There was plenty of action to be found around the village, from competitors spotted calming their nerves with pints in the local hotel, to an American visitor who accidentally caused controversy by dressing as a box of Scott’s Porage Oats – rolled oats of the kind not allowed in competition, and a rival to the event’s sponsors, Hamlyns.
By the afternoon, the hall was full of cooking aromas and the crowd full of whisky and porridge as they took their seats once more to see who would walk away victorious. There was a minor upset when the reigning champion, Seljom, missed out on the final, but a surprise win for McTeague saw him through to the cook-off despite his earlier woes.
Once the top six had taken to the hob one last time, though, it was the Netherlands national champion, Gina Saarberg, who emerged victorious in the traditional competition, with the speciality prize going to Reid for his cannoli.
“I’m at a loss for words,” Saarberg said as she clutched her Golden Spurtle. “To be here was already such a win in the first place. This is a beautiful community, so of course I’m very happy I won, but it’s also just a pleasure to be here.”

articles.title_orig: Free World Music Ensemble debuts in Johns Creek Oct. 10
articles.title_zh: Free World Music Ensemble debuts in Johns Creek Oct. 10
articles.content_orig:
The UGA Middle East Ensemble, a Middle Eastern and African instrumental group, will be among the groups performing Oct. 10 at the World Music Ensemble at Johns Creek United Methodist Church.
A unique musical endeavor will debut in Johns Creek Oct. 10. The World Music Ensemble, a fully instrumental grassroots event, will showcase traditional, folk, Indigenous and classical instruments from around the world as well as from Georgia's own communities.
Designed for musical groups with 10 or fewer members, the WME creates a rich, exceptional, one-of-a-kind listening experience for the community by spotlighting established musicians as well as student performers.
Presented by the nonprofit organization Arts On The Creek in partnership with Fulton County Arts & Culture, the free inaugural event will be Saturday, Oct. 10, from 11 a.m. to 8 p.m. at Johns Creek United Methodist Church, 11180 Medlock Bridge Road.
The lineup, which reflects a range of presentations and is updated regularly, includes:
Wontanara, an African percussion group
Bahar, an Indian strings group
Apuinka, an Andean instrument group
University of Georgia Middle East Ensemble, a Middle Eastern and African instrumental group
Musik21 Conservatory, a local classical ensemble from Vienna
UGA Chinese Ensemble, featuring Chinese instruments
Atlanta Metropolitan Orchestra, a classical orchestra
Phoenix School of Irish Arts, representing instrumental music from Ireland
Focused on arts and culture throughout Fulton County, the WME seeks to celebrate and preserve the rich heritage of traditional instrumental music from various cultures, "including musical traditions represented within the many cultural communities that call Fulton County home," said Nilendra Chanda, the WME's director.
The nonprofit event will give musicians of all ages a platform to showcase instruments from diverse cultures and histories. Through this # OneFulton event, the WME, presented by a public-private partnership, will foster cultural appreciation and musical education.
"The event will use the universal language of instrumental music to bring audiences together across cultural and linguistic boundaries while promoting cultural appreciation, arts education, community connection and the preservation of cultural heritage," Chanda said. "There is no headliner, no big entertainment company and no social agenda; it is simply about coming together and getting to know each other through music."
Chanda said the "collage of cultures will be more evident in the coming years" and described the WME's debut as a "small and humble start with big dreams."
Sponsorships are available, and applications are open, but space is limited.
For more information, visit ArtsOnTheCreek.org .

articles.title_orig: Trump launches ‘Super Intelligence Force’ after calls for AI slowdown
articles.title_zh: Trump launches ‘Super Intelligence Force’ after calls for AI slowdown
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump on Sunday announced the leadership and duties of a “Super Intelligence Force,” which he said will “ensure that America continues to lead the world” when it comes to artificial intelligence.
The president said in his announcement on Truth Social that the task force will “protect the interests” and “improve the lives” of Americans. He said it will coordinate the government’s engagement with consumers, public interest groups, religious organizations, infrastructure providers and AI companies.
The group will be led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, Chairman of the Federal Trade Commission Andrew Ferguson, Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering Emil Michael, and Director of the Office of Personnel Management Scott Kupor. The task force will report to Trump and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, the president said.
Trump announced last month that he was planning to create an “AI Force” and name an AI czar as the government faces growing calls to impose guardrails on the technology’s rapid development. CNN reported Friday that Trump was expected to tap Clayton to lead the group.
The announcement detailing the task force comes in the wake of episodes that have raised widespread safety concerns tied to AI, including AI agents going rogue and attempting to hack into federal databases.
The president has made clear that he considers outpacing China and preserving AI-driven economic gains a higher priority than addressing growing public concerns, and previously referred to fears over AI as being a “hoax.” His support for the technology comes amid widespread frustrations over the data centers used to support it, which are shaking up midterm races.
The president hosted top AI executives at the White House last week. The group signed a new commitment aimed at better “self-policing” their companies’ AI models, arguing that the light-touch approach represents the best way to balance safety concerns with the president’s desire to accelerate a technology he’s dubbed “Super Intelligence.”
“I’m seeing tremendous self-policing, and they understand that they have to self-police,” Trump told reporters. “These models are very complex and, again, I believe they’re going to be used for the good.”
When asked about AI during his confirmation hearing to lead the US intelligence community, Clayton said the technology is a “game changer.”
“When something’s both an opportunity and a threat, you better get your arms around it,” Clayton said.
Kupor said Sunday on X that “the U.S. will continue to lead in SI to enhance the well-being of all Americans.”
Michael wrote on X that the Pentagon “has seen what is possible when red tape is removed and America’s best technology is rapidly put into action.”
“Working alongside America’s leading technology companies, we are putting the most advanced SI capabilities into the hands of our warfighters at speed and scale,” he said.
This story has been updated with additional information.
CNN’s Hadas Gold, Alayna Treene and Adam Cancryn contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Bosnia votes in one of world’s most complicated general elections
articles.title_zh: Bosnia votes in one of world’s most complicated general elections
articles.content_orig:
Early results in the race to elect Bosnia and Herzegovina’s tripartite presidency show leftist and nationalist candidates leading the count.
The early returns emerged as polls closed across Bosnia and Herzegovina on Sunday, concluding a general election at national and regional levels that could significantly impact the country’s European Union membership bid.
Leftist moderate Denis Becirovic and nationalist figures Zeljka Cvijanovic and Darijana Filipovic were leading the race as the Central Election Commission released preliminary results shortly after polls closed.
Becirovic, representing the Social Democratic Party (SDP-BiH), led the contest for the Bosniak seat. Cvijanovic of the Alliance of Independent Social Democrats (SNSD) led the race for the Serb seat. The Croatian Democratic Union’s (HDZ-BiH) Filipovic led the field for the Croat seat.
About 3.4 million voters were eligible to vote in Sunday’s election to choose the three members of the country’s multiethnic presidency, legislators for the national Parliament and heads of institutions for the country’s two entities: the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina (FBiH) and Republika Srpska.
Bosnia’s complex web of governing institutions was created by a United States-brokered peace agreement in 1995 in an effort to manage the ethnic divisions between Muslim Bosniaks, Orthodox Serbs and Catholic Croats that gave rise to the 1992-95 war.
The major parties’ repeated focus on war-era rhetoric and division was frustrating for some voters, activist Adi Selman of the Karton Revolucija protest group told the AFP news agency.
“I don’t think these new elections in Bosnia will change anything,” the 34-year-old said in the northern Bosnian town of Tuzla, ahead of the vote.
“The choice is limited to political parties that have already been around for 30 years and basically pick up votes by harping on about war, tensions, divisions and the past.”
“Bosnia and Herzegovina is dead; it is an impossible country,” Republika Srpska’s former President Milorad Dodik told the final rally of his right-wing Alliance of Independent Social Democrats (SNSD) in the entity’s capital Banja Luka late on Friday.
In the FBiH, Bosniak parties are pushing for a stronger central state, with incumbent Bosniak presidency member Becirovic pledging a renewed path to the EU and NATO.
The EU granted Bosnia candidate status in December 2022, but accession negotiations scheduled for 2024 were delayed as Brussels demanded the country pass stronger anticorruption laws and reform its judicial system.
Croat nationalist parties are also pushing for electoral reform, demanding a greater say in choosing the Croat member of the presidency in the entity they share with the more numerous Bosniaks.
Meanwhile, Russia is accused of slowing down the country’s path towards joining the EU, while also holding close ties with the SNSD, which favours secession for Republika Srpska, which is dominated by ethnic Serbs.
This general election is the first in the country in which new electronic tools are being used to scan ballot papers and carry out biometric fingerprint verification to reduce voter fraud.

articles.title_orig: What to Know About the Medical Plane That Went Missing Near Nantucket
articles.title_zh: What to Know About the Medical Plane That Went Missing Near Nantucket
articles.content_orig:
The US Coast Guard continued to search Sunday for six passengers who were aboard a medical transport flight that vanished while flying from Bermuda to Boston the prior day, authorities said.
The jet went missing early Saturday morning and searchers found debris about 20 miles off the coast of Nantucket, but the people aboard the jet have yet to be located among the recovery.
“Our priority is to locate the six personnel and aircraft,” Matthew Lake, the Northeast district commander for the US Coast Guard, said at a press briefing Sunday at the Coast Guard’s Boston base. The Coast Guard is also still searching for the jet’s black box.
Search crews covered more than 2,800 square miles over about 50 hours, Lake said.
Officials said crews are using boats, planes, and helicopters, and weather conditions Sunday have been favorable for searching. The water near where the debris was found is about 80 to 90 feet deep and the Coast Guard said it is working to deploy some craft equipped with sonar to help.
“It is a rather large area to search, but we have sufficient assets where we are saturating the area,” said Captain John McTamney, the Coast Guard’s Northeast district chief of response.
The Coast Guard launched the search off Nantucket after the transport flight disappeared early Saturday. Air traffic controllers in New York and the Boston air traffic control center in Nashua, N.H., had struggled to communicate with the jet as it plunged toward the Atlantic Ocean.
“You’re coming in blind? Is that what you said?” a controller asked the pilot at about 12:46 a.m. “Are you declaring an emergency, or no?”
The pilot’s response, according to a recording captured by LiveATC.net, was not audible.
The airplane, a Gulfstream G100 that took off from Bermuda late Friday, was carrying a patient and family member as well as a four-person crew.
As the jet approached Nantucket, its pilot reported electrical failures, according to radio transmissions . Data from the website FlightAware show the plane descended thousands of feet within three minutes.
Shortly afterward, around 1 a.m., it disappeared from radar entirely.
The crew members are Canadian citizens and the passengers are Bermudian nationals, according to Clarence Togeretz, operations manager for Latitude Air Ambulance, the company in Ontario that operates the Gulfstream G100.
Steven MacKinnon, the leader of Canada’s public transportation agency, declined to identify the people on board the flight. The Bermuda Gazette reported that the two passengers aboard were a medical patient and a companion.
In a statement, the Bermudian government said it was in touch with the families of the passengers and US search crews.
“We are praying that all six people will be found safe,” said Bermuda Premier David Burt.
The plane left L. F. Wade International Airport in Bermuda for the 800-mile flight to Boston at 11:41 p.m. on Friday, said Ciara Eve, an airport spokesperson. Bermuda, a self-governing British territory, is one hour ahead of Eastern Daylight Time.
As the jet descended toward the Atlantic, air traffic controllers asked to confirm whether they were declaring an emergency.
“You’re coming in a little weak so I didn’t hear what your response was, if you were declaring an emergency or not,” the New York air traffic controller said. He later confirmed the pilot declared an emergency, but struggled to reestablish contact with the aircraft.
The controller asked the pilot of a second plane whether the Gulfstream G100 aircraft was visible on its anti-collision system. But the second plane was flying at a much higher altitude and couldn’t pick up signs of the jet, the pilot said.
A Boston Center air traffic controller also struggled to make contact with the jet and locate the aircraft, according to a recording from LiveATC.net.
“I believe we may have lost an aircraft,” the air traffic controller said. “We lost everything on him ... like a long time ago.”
For much of the flight, the Gulfstream jet traveled at about 24,000 feet, but at about 1:04 a.m., FlightAware data show the plane descended 13,000 feet within three minutes.
With the plane about 80 miles south of Nantucket at 1:06 a.m., a dispatcher at Logan International Airport directed crews to stage on the runway for the plane. She said it was due to land in 15 minutes and had lost “radio and radar,” according to radio transmissions captured by Broadcastify.
Emergency crews got into position and waited.
At 1:20 a.m., the Federal Aviation Administration issued an alert, an agency spokesperson said. The plane wouldn’t land at Logan, and a search and rescue mission had been launched.
On the runway at Logan, the Massport Fire Rescue commander heard a radio transmission reporting that air traffic control said it could no longer see the plane on the radar.
“I don’t know if you monitored the tower radio, but the tower lost radar contact with this aircraft,” the commander radioed at about 1:36 a.m.
“Received, I do have it. I was listening,” the dispatcher said.
Emergency crews on the runway were ordered back to their headquarters. At 2 a.m., the FAA alerted the US Coast Guard of the missing plane.
On Nantucket, police checked the island’s airport for the missing jet but found nothing, said Lieutenant Angus MacVicar.
At sunrise, officers and the harbormaster began combing Nantucket’s southern shoreline aboard ATVs in search of signs of the plane, he said.
Until the jet’s black box is located, it remains difficult to know exactly what happened onboard before the plane vanished, said Mike Slack, a pilot and aviation lawyer.
But flight tracking data that shows the plane plummeted at a rate of several thousand feet per minute suggests the aircraft likely lost control, he said.
“Clearly, an aircraft descending at over 4,000 feet a minute from 24,000 feet to 11,000 is out of control,” said Slack, managing partner of Slack Davis, a personal injury law firm in Texas. “No pilot would do that if they were in control of the aircraft.”
A Gulfstream G100 is a “high-performance” jet, but can be difficult to manage if control is lost, especially at night over the ocean, Slack said. In these types of planes, pilots typically might have about 10 to 20 seconds to react to a problem, he said.
But with the aircraft descending so quickly, the G-loads would have been significant, making it extremely difficult for crew members — if they were still conscious — to take action, he said. The plane also could have experienced a “catastrophic structural failure” during the rapid descent, he added.
The search for the Boston-bound jet is unfolding in waters south of Massachusetts, where another plane went missing 25 years ago when John F. Kennedy Jr. crashed his single-engine plane west of Martha’s Vineyard.
His wife, Carolyn Besette-Kennedy, and his sister-in-law, Lauren Bessette, were also on board. After five days of searching, the US Navy helped recover the bodies of all three victims from 116 feet of water, still strapped in their seats.
Lake said he did not want to speculate on the Navy’s involvement in the current search for the medical jet.
“That gets into salvage operations, which is beyond what the Coast Guard would do during this phase of the operation,” he said.
Governor Maura Healey said Saturday her “thoughts and prayers go out to all on board and all involved.”
“We’ll do whatever we can as a state to support efforts there and work with the Coast Guard,” Healey said at a labor rally in Dorchester.
The Coast Guard will continue to search the debris field until they are confident there are no survivors remaining on the surface of the water, McTamney said.
This weekend’s incident comes just days after another medical transport flight crashed off the coast of Southern California , leaving three dead. Five people were aboard the helicopter when it went down near Catalina Island, about 20 miles southwest of Los Angeles. Two survivors were recovered from the water and transported to the hospital.
Chris Van Buski

articles.title_orig: Cornell University to take ‘serious look’ at fraternities after rape allegations
articles.title_zh: Cornell University to take ‘serious look’ at fraternities after rape allegations
articles.content_orig:
Ivy League school’s president promises action after woman alleged she was drugged ⁠and raped by fraternity members
Cornell University will examine the role of fraternities and sororities on campus after an outcry over the school’s handling ⁠of a student’s rape allegations, the Ivy League school’s president has said.
A civil lawsuit filed last month by the woman , who ⁠alleges she was drugged ⁠and raped in ​2024 by several members of the Chi Phi fraternity, has prompted outrage and soul-searching at Cornell over its campus culture at the ⁠school in Ithaca, New York.
In a video message on Saturday, the Cornell University president, Michael Kotlikoff, said the school would take steps to prevent a similar situation in the ⁠future. That included “a serious look at the role of fraternities and sororities in campus life,” Kotlikoff said.
“At ​their best, these organisations can provide ‌students with friendship, belonging, mentorship ‌and a powerful sense of community,” he said. “But being part of a group can never diminish ‌individual responsibility.“
The university would seek input, he said, from students, alumni and others on how to “preserve what is valuable about Greek life while strengthening individual accountability, transparency and a culture in which every member understands their responsibility to protect the safety and wellbeing of others”.
The lawsuit against Cornell, seven fraternity members and others, alleges that the school failed to adequately punish ‌some of the accused students.
The accused men have denied all wrongdoing, the New York Times has reported.
Cornell has defended its handling of the matter, saying it launched ​a comprehensive investigation and barred the Chi Phi fraternity from campus. The school said it imposed a range of disciplinary measures, including expulsions.
But “we must do better”, Kotlikoff said. “We don’t have all the answers, but we are committed to investigating and finding the answers our community deserves.”
He vowed that ⁠university officials would “be more transparent” about their actions related to the 2024 incident, but ​he did not detail ​specific initiatives that the university would take. “In ​the coming weeks, we will create additional opportunities for members of our ​community to ask ‌questions and hear directly ​from university leadership,” ​he said.
The case has reignited scrutiny of how law enforcement and universities handle sexual assault complaints, with students questioning whether processes are enough to protect them. It has also drawn the attention of New York state officials, who have appointed a special prosecutor to investigate.
As the special prosecutor, Letitia James, the New York attorney general, investigates, new attention has been drawn to the findings of a state-mandated sexual violence survey conducted by Cornell in 2025, which found that 35% of female undergraduates who completed the survey reported that they had experienced nonconsensual sexual contact while at the university.
The 2025 version of the survey was the first to specifically include unwanted choking or strangulation in the definition of nonconsensual sexual contact involving force or incapacitation that students were asked about, in addition to nonconsensual penetration and/or sexual touching.’
Guardian staff contributed reporting

articles.title_orig: Trump names national intelligence director Jay Clayton to lead a new federal AI task force
articles.title_zh: Trump names national intelligence director Jay Clayton to lead a new federal AI task force
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump on Sunday announced the leadership and duties of a “Super Intelligence Force,” which he said will “ensure that America continues to lead the world” when it comes to artificial intelligence.
The president said in his announcement on Truth Social that the task force will “protect the interests” and “improve the lives” of Americans. He said it will coordinate the government’s engagement with consumers, public interest groups, religious organizations, infrastructure providers and AI companies.
The group will be led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, Chairman of the Federal Trade Commission Andrew Ferguson, Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering Emil Michael, and Director of the Office of Personnel Management Scott Kupor. The task force will report to Trump and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, the president said.
Trump announced last month that he was planning to create an “AI Force” and name an AI czar as the government faces growing calls to impose guardrails on the technology’s rapid development. CNN reported Friday that Trump was expected to tap Clayton to lead the group.
The announcement detailing the task force comes in the wake of episodes that have raised widespread safety concerns tied to AI, including AI agents going rogue and attempting to hack into federal databases.
The president has made clear that he considers outpacing China and preserving AI-driven economic gains a higher priority than addressing growing public concerns, and previously referred to fears over AI as being a “hoax.” His support for the technology comes amid widespread frustrations over the data centers used to support it, which are shaking up midterm races.
The president hosted top AI executives at the White House last week. The group signed a new commitment aimed at better “self-policing” their companies’ AI models, arguing that the light-touch approach represents the best way to balance safety concerns with the president’s desire to accelerate a technology he’s dubbed “Super Intelligence.”
“I’m seeing tremendous self-policing, and they understand that they have to self-police,” Trump told reporters. “These models are very complex and, again, I believe they’re going to be used for the good.”
When asked about AI during his confirmation hearing to lead the US intelligence community, Clayton said the technology is a “game changer.”
“When something’s both an opportunity and a threat, you better get your arms around it,” Clayton said.
Kupor said Sunday on X that “the U.S. will continue to lead in SI to enhance the well-being of all Americans.”
Michael wrote on X that the Pentagon “has seen what is possible when red tape is removed and America’s best technology is rapidly put into action.”
“Working alongside America’s leading technology companies, we are putting the most advanced SI capabilities into the hands of our warfighters at speed and scale,” he said.
This story has been updated with additional information.
CNN’s Hadas Gold, Alayna Treene and Adam Cancryn contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Port Canaveral’s next mega cruise ship is a step closer to sailing. Meet the MSC World Atlantic
articles.title_zh: Port Canaveral’s next mega cruise ship is a step closer to sailing. Meet the MSC World Atlantic
articles.content_orig:
Christie Zizo , Digital Journalist
Port Canaveral is getting two new ships in 2027, and one of them just hit a major milestone.
This week, MSC Cruises new ship, MSC World Atlantic , had its first float-out, moving from the construction dock to the harbor at the Chantiers de l’Atlantique shipyard in France.
Crews still need to work on the interiors of the vessel, including public spaces.
The 25th ship in the MSC Cruises fleet, the MSC World Atlantic will be able to hold 6,758 guests, with 2,582 cabins. The ship also has seven pools, including adults-only pools, an aqua park, a ropes course, a family-friendly clubhouse with bumper cars, roller skating and basketball, several entertainment venues, and several restaurants.
The World Atlantic will be available for 7-night and 14-night Caribbean itineraries from Port Canaveral, starting November 2027.
The other ship coming to Port Canaveral next year, the Carnival Festivale, is expected to begin sailing in May.
Copyright 2026 by WKMG ClickOrlando - All rights reserved.
Christie joined the ClickOrlando team in November 2021.  She cultivated her political reporting skills at Spectrum News 13, and before that at UCF. She spends her spare time with her beagle, Lulu, finding hidden gems around Central Florida, playing the violin and indulging her love for all things geek with her friends.

articles.title_orig: Sybiha on bridge attacks: World must make it clear to Russia that it must stop escalation
articles.title_zh: Sybiha on bridge attacks: World must make it clear to Russia that it must stop escalation
articles.content_orig:
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha called on partners to respond decisively to Russian terror, strengthen Ukraine's air defense and impose effective sanctions on Russia's defense industry.
He said this in a post on X , according to Ukrinform.
The foreign minister said that this week marked a new chapter in Russia's campaign of all-day terror against civilians and that after targeting food depots, retail chains, pharmacy warehouses, and vital databases, Russia is now going after bridges.
"They are important lifelines that keep the country functioning, connect communities, allow people to get to work and access essential services," Sybiha said.
The minister recalled that over the past few days, Russia had struck two bridges in Kyiv six times, right when civilian traffic was using them and metro trains were crossing.
"The world cannot simply watch and wait – we urge strong reactions by our partners. Both in words and deeds. Make clear to Moscow that it must stop its escalation and terror – and engage in diplomacy and peace efforts," Sybiha said.
He also called on allies to strengthen Ukraine's air defense, impose effective sanctions on Russia's military-industrial complex, and add to sanctions lists the individuals and organizations that enable the regime to continue committing its crimes.
As reported, two people were injured in a Russian strike on Kyiv's Northern Bridge on October 4.

articles.title_orig: Russia strikes Kyiv bridge as German chancellor visits Ukraine in show of support
articles.title_zh: Russia strikes Kyiv bridge as German chancellor visits Ukraine in show of support
articles.content_orig:
Attack shortly after Friedrich Merz arrived on unannounced visit intended to underline Germany’s backing
Russia has struck another major bridge in Kyiv as the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz , arrived in the capital in a show of support for Ukraine.
A Russian drone hit Kyiv’s key Northern Bridge over the Dnipro River, marking the fourth consecutive day that Russia has targeted bridges used by tens of thousands of residents commuting between the city’s two banks. Video footage showed cars driving across the bridge as the drone plunged into the roadway and exploded in a burst of fire. Two people were injured in the strike, said Kyiv’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko.
The attack came shortly after Merz arrived in the city on an unannounced visit intended to underline Germany’s backing of Ukraine, as the country enters one of the most precarious periods since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.
Germany has become Ukraine’s biggest provider of military aid since Merz entered office in May 2025, surpassing the US as American support has declined.
Kyiv has come under near-constant attack from Russia’s new jet-powered drones in recent weeks, as an intensifying strike campaign increasingly disrupts everyday life in the capital and threatens to leave the city without power this winter.
On his visit, Merz announced that Germany would fund the joint production of drones designed to intercept Russia’s jet-powered drones, adding that “significant technical breakthroughs” in recent weeks were speeding up production.
“This will quickly and tangibly strengthen Ukraine’s air defence,” he said. “And this strengthening is urgently needed.”
The German leader got a taste of the new reality of daily life in the Ukrainian capital. Air-raid sirens sounded repeatedly during his visit, including as Volodymyr Zelenskyy showed him the badly damaged National Academy of Sciences building, where a Russian drone strike killed two people last week .
The Ukrainian president told Merz that people in Kyiv were suffering “terrible nights and days” from the relentless attacks, and called Ukraine’s Russian adversaries “absolute barbarians”.
“We can see the entire pointlessness of this war at this place,” said Merz, adding as he arrived that Ukraine “needs all our support in the coming weeks”. “If Russia is not stopped, its war machine will sooner or later turn against us,” he said.
Russia had already damaged Kyiv’s Northern Bridge and repeatedly struck its Southern Bridge. Although the crossings remain standing, repeated attacks and the threat of further strikes have prompted the city’s authorities to restrict or suspend traffic on five of the city’s six road bridges over the Dnipro, causing temporary closures and large traffic jams.
If Moscow succeeds in seriously damaging Kyiv’s bridges, it could create a logistical nightmare for the city of 3 million people, whose crossings over the Dnipro were last destroyed on a large scale as Nazi German forces retreated in 1943. More than a third of residents live on the left bank while much of the city’s employment and infrastructure is concentrated on the right.
The attacks form part of a broader Russian campaign against civilian and industrial infrastructure inside Ukraine. In recent weeks, strikes have hit logistics hubs, railway lines, datacentres, medical storage facilities and steel plants, alongside a sustained assault on the country’s energy system that is expected to intensify over the winter.
“He [Putin] is counting on constant escalation. He wants this very much,” Zelenskyy said at a press conference alongside Merz. “This is an answer to everyone – to those who believe that all you have to do is simply ask Putin and he will end the war for real. It won’t happen, simply.”
Russia’s foreign ministry on Saturday warned foreign nationals and diplomatic staff against remaining in or travelling to Ukraine. “Responsibility for any possible adverse consequences lies entirely with those who choose to disregard this warning,” the ministry said.
A number of foreign ambassadors, including Germany’s, responded on social media that they intended to remain in Kyiv.
“The EU delegation is staying,” the European Union ambassador, Katarína Mathernová, wrote on X on Sunday. “Threatening us will not stop Europe’s support for Ukraine. It only reminds us why that support matters.”
In Moscow, some pro-war commenters noted with glee that the Russian strikes had continued despite Merz’s arrival. “Russia used to pause strikes on Kyiv during visits by European politicians. Not any more,” wrote Sergei Markov, a prominent pro-war commentator.
The trip is Merz’s second to Ukraine since becoming chancellor. He has been among Kyiv’s most outspoken supporters in Europe and a leading voice warning about Russia’s hybrid campaign against other nations.
Last month, Germany formally accused Moscow of being behind a suspected plot targeting Leipzig/Halle airport , a key logistics hub for western military aid to Ukraine. But Merz is also facing growing discontent at home over his support for Ukraine, as his approval ratings fall.
Germany’s far left and far right are sceptical of support for Ukraine and want Berlin to scale back aid. The pressure has intensified as the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) has made big electoral gains .
Alice Weidel, the AfD’s co-leader, wrote in a social media post: “Merz is travelling to Ukraine on Germany’s national holiday and promising further billions in German taxpayer money that is missing from the pension and health insurance funds, while Germany is mired in its worst energy crisis.”

articles.title_orig: Yemeni and Saudi forces launch counteroffensive against the Houthis
articles.title_zh: Yemeni and Saudi forces launch counteroffensive against the Houthis
articles.content_orig:
Iran-aligned Houthi forces reportedly took control of Yemeni Presidential Leadership Council Chairman Rashad al-Alimi’s residence after government forces withdrew from al-Aloum and several areas of Taiz Governorate, according to a local news outlet cited by Yemen News Portal.
The claim, if confirmed, would mark a symbolic blow to Yemen’s internationally recognized government as it says military operations are underway to retake remaining territory from the Houthis.
The report comes after al-Alimi announced the start of operations to restore state control across Yemen, while government-aligned forces reported strikes against Houthi targets in Sanaa and Saada.
The fighting has intensified as part of the regional spillover from the Iran war, with the Houthis declaring a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia in July and launching attacks on Saudi territory and shipping.
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said it killed a Hamas Nukhba operative Sunday who led a group that claimed humanitarian status while funding terror networks that targeted its troops.
Saqr Nabil Musa Qaisi had taken part in the Oct. 7 massacre while serving as director of a Turkish aid organization, the IDF said.
"He also served as the director of the Turkish organization Deniz Feneri, which presents itself as a humanitarian aid organization but in practice maintains ties with senior figures in Hamas’ leadership and with elements within the Turkish leadership," the IDF said on X .
“Recently, and throughout the war, the terrorist advanced terrorist activities against Israeli civilians & IDF troops and worked to restore Hamas’ capabilities, in systematic violation of the ceasefire."
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi pushed back Sunday against reports that Tehran’s U.N. delegation had been forced out of the United States, insisting all diplomats left "as scheduled" following the U.N. General Assembly.
Araghchi's remarks came after reports emerged that Secretary of State Marco Rubio had demanded on Sept. 28 that the Iranian delegation immediately leave the United States at the end of the summit and as sideline talks between Washington and Tehran stalled.
“All Iranian diplomats who attended the U.N. General Assembly, except one who departed earlier, left as scheduled,” Araghchi said on X .
“Taking pride in fake diplomat 'expulsion' is inappropriate for the head of any diplomatic corps,” he added. "It oozes of desperation and defeat, and is inconsistent with UN host nation obligations."
Australian counterterrorism authorities are investigating the alleged FlyDubai hijacking suspect’s links to the country after officials said the co-pilot stabbed the captain and tried to seize control of a flight bound for Israel.
The Victorian Joint Counter Terrorism Team, which includes federal police, state police and the ASIO intelligence agency, is “ investigating the man’s links to Australia ,” an Australian Federal Police spokesperson told Reuters.
The Financial Times reported Sunday that attacker had allegedly visited what it described as radical mosques and extremist websites while in Australia, citing two people familiar with the investigation. Australian intelligence services held a file on the individual, according to the Financial Times.
Two sources briefed on the investigation told Reuters the co-pilot studied at a university in Melbourne, while a third source said he studied at RMIT University about a decade ago. RMIT declined to comment.
The co-pilot of FlyDubai flight FZ1073 attacked the pilot with an emergency crash ax, the United Arab Emirates prosecutor general said Saturday, calling the incident a “terrorist attack.”
Two sources identified the co-pilot to Reuters as Omani national Hamam Al-Hamami. Israeli officials have said the co-pilot was from Oman, but UAE authorities and FlyDubai have not publicly disclosed his identity.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the co-pilot had undergone radical Islamist indoctrination and was “clearly suicidal,” and ordered a review of “all security aspects” involving foreign civilian aviation to Israel.
Reuters contributed to this report.
Iran’s oil minister has resigned , state media reported, as the country faces mounting pressure on its energy sector during the war with the United States.
President Masoud Pezeshkian accepted the resignation of Oil Minister Mohsen Paknejad and appointed Hamid Bovard as acting oil minister, according to Iranian state media cited by a local news outlet via a public Telegram board.
The reported shakeup comes as Iran’s oil exports and regional energy flows remain under intense strain from the conflict, including disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Gulf.
The Oil Ministry change also follows OPEC+ sources telling Reuters that Gulf producers have been pumping far below output targets as the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran continues to disrupt exports.
Reuters contributed to this report.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has ordered a comprehensive review of security surrounding foreign civilian aviation to Israel, his office said Sunday.
Netanyahu instructed National Security Council Director Shmuel Ben Ezra to appoint an examiner to review “all aspects of security” related to foreign civil aviation to Israel , according to a translated statement from the prime minister’s Office.
"Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has instructed National Security Council Director Shmuel Ben Ezra to appoint an examiner to conduct a comprehensive review of all aspects of security relating to foreign civil aviation to Israel."
The move comes amid heightened aviation security concerns during the Iran war, including recent allegations that a co-pilot attacked a pilot aboard a FlyDubai flight bound for Israel.
U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee said Sunday that the FlyDubai incident was under “a very intense investigation” and called it a “terrorist act.”
A co-pilot’s attack on a FlyDubai pilot with an ax was a “terrorist act,” U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee said Sunday, praising Israeli plumber Yaniv Hayoun for helping save 174 people aboard the flight.
“He really is an incredible hero. Had he not acted 174 people, including 30 children, would absolutely have been lost," Huckabee told Fox News' "Sunday Briefing." "And the fact that he acted without hesitation that he went and subdued the co-pilot, then, jumped on the yoke of the plane and pulled it back, not because he'd ever had a flying lesson in his life, but he had watched a television show called 'Air Disaster' and somehow intuitively knew what to do. It was one miracle after another."
The investigation will be "very intense," according to Huckabee.
“ It was a terrorist act : He tried to kill everybody on that plane," he continued.
"He would have died, too, but he didn't care. I think it's one of the most amazing stories. How this would have been horrible. Tragedy got diverted – not because there were armed security , but because there were just brave people who said, not today, Satan. And they took him down.”
Huckabee said he invited Hayoun to the U.S. Embassy after seeing him say he wanted to thank President Donald Trump, then gave him a MAGA hat signed by Trump that Huckabee had kept in a display case.
“This guy is a hero. He has earned that hat,” Huckabee said.

articles.title_orig: Cornell president calls gang rape allegations ‘deeply disturbing’
articles.title_zh: Cornell president calls gang rape allegations ‘deeply disturbing’
articles.content_orig:
Pedestrians walk on the campus at Cornell University in Ithaca, N.Y., Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026. Matt Rourke/AP hide caption
Cornell University's president has said the institution "must do better" following a civil lawsuit filed in recent weeks alleging a gang rape at a fraternity house in 2024.
In an eight-minute video statement released by Cornell on Saturday, president Michael I. Kotlikoff acknowledged questions over the university's handling of the female student's sexual assault allegations, which were reported to Cornell University Police and school officials a few weeks after she said the attack happened.
"I want to acknowledge something that can be difficult for an institution to say. We don't have all the answers, but we are committed to investigating and finding the answers our community deserves," Kotlikoff said in the statement. "We must do everything we can to prevent what happened to Jane Doe and everyone before her and anyone after her from ever happening again."
A former Cornell student, identified as Jane Doe, sued the university and seven former students last month, alleging she was drugged and repeatedly raped at the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024, when she was 20 years old. Attorneys for some of the men have denied the accusations.
Kotlikoff called recent days one of the most difficult weeks in Cornell's history.
"What happened to Jane Doe in 2024 is deeply disturbing and will weigh heavily on our community for years to come. My heart aches when I think of what she experienced," he said. "It raises heartbreaking and troubling issues about sexual assault, dehumanization and aspects of party culture, alcohol and drug use. It also raises questions around the investigations conducted after the allegations were reported."
Jane Doe first reported her claims to Cornell University police and university Title IX investigators shortly after the alleged incident. She also reported the sexual assault to the campus health clinic.
According to the lawsuit filed against Cornell, Chi Phi fraternity, seven fraternity members and other defendants in September, Jane Doe said she consented initially to sexual contact with two men she knew at the fraternity house while intoxicated. She alleges, as the night went on, she was then drugged and raped by multiple men, and could not give consent.
The Tompkins County district attorney declined to file charges. He has said recently he didn't receive full transcripts from Jane Doe's interview with Cornell Police, in which she clearly stated she had been raped.
"As a community, we must foster a culture in which sexual assault is inexcusable and ensure our community is empowered and understands informed consent, body autonomy and prevention. We all have a role to play in keeping each other safe," said Kotlikoff in his video message.
Last week, Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed New York State Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor in the case and condemned the handling of the investigations. Kotlikoff said he welcomes the governor's decision, and that the university's board of trustees will soon announce plans for an independent review by an outside law firm into "all aspects of Cornell's handling" of the case.
"We will also lend our full support to legislative efforts to change New York's sexual assault laws. You have my commitment that this will not be a moment that passes," he said.
Kotlikoff added the university would take immediate actions to be more transparent, strengthen sexual assault prevention and education efforts and substance use resources. He said the university will also take a serious look at the role of sororities and fraternities in campus life.

articles.title_orig: Dabo Swinney 'absolutely' thinks Clemson can still be an ACC title contender after 41-13 loss to No. 4 Miami
articles.title_zh: Dabo Swinney 'absolutely' thinks Clemson can still be an ACC title contender after 41-13 loss to No. 4 Miami
articles.content_orig:
Clemson looked like the furthest thing from an ACC title contender Saturday night against No. 4 Miami. But that's not stopping Tigers coach Dabo Swinney from believing in his team's chances.
When asked after the 41-13 loss if he thought his team could still compete for the ACC title, Swinney was unequivocal.
"Absolutely. Absolutely. We were 3-1 coming in, we've lost to two really good teams, but we're still progressing," Swinney said. "We're just going to keep battling. We'll keep battling. Got a lot of opportunity ahead."
Yes, Clemson has lost to two really good teams in No. 4 Miami and No. 11 LSU. But it's lost to those really good teams by 69 combined points. That's not nice.
To be an ACC contender, Clemson needs to be a really good team. Or, at least show that it's capable of beating a really good team. Neither is close to happening at the moment.
Clemson's offense is being led by freshman quarterback Tait Reynolds, and it's clear that he's still learning the ropes of being a college quarterback. Reynolds was 29-of-44 passing for 295 yards and an interception against the Hurricanes. It was the first time he had thrown over 29 passes or thrown for over 215 yards in a single game.
The run game that Clemson relied on in Week 4 against Cal was nonexistent against Miami. The Tigers rushed 31 times for 55 yards on Saturday night. In its Week 1 loss to LSU, Clemson rushed 26 times for 40 yards. If you stop the Clemson run game, you have a really good chance of winning the game.
"And hey, we're 3-2; we hoped we'd be 5-0 right now, 4-1 at worst," Swinney continued. "But we're 3-2. But we're, what, 2-1 in the ACC? We're right here. We're right there. We just gotta dig in, man. Gotta go play. There's a lot of opportunity for this team."
That opportunity to make up ground in the ACC standings won't come until Oct. 24. After a bye week in Week 6, the Tigers host Charleston Southern on Oct. 17.
If there is a silver lining for Clemson, it's that there are no more ranked teams on the Tigers' schedule the rest of the season. After Charleston Southern, Clemson has Virginia Tech, Florida State, Syracuse, Georgia Tech, Duke and South Carolina. Wins in all six of those will get Clemson back to the ACC championship game … and likely set up a rematch with a far superior Miami.

articles.title_orig: This toolless modular lever-action wallet is the coolest I’ve stuck to my phone
articles.title_zh: This toolless modular lever-action wallet is the coolest I’ve stuck to my phone
articles.content_orig:
Pull the lever to fan your cards with the OhSnap Wallet 2.
Pull the lever to fan your cards with the OhSnap Wallet 2.
This toolless modular lever-action wallet is the coolest I’ve stuck to my phone.
Remember when I tested the ultra-thin and convenient OhSnap Snap Grip Stand and liked it so much I bought my own ? Now, OhSnap has a magnetic lever-action card wallet that can stack with that stand. It’s the coolest wallet I’ve ever stuck to my phone.
Pull the integrated springy lever, and your cards fan out. Want a thicker or thinner wallet? Press in the right place and it comes apart without tools, letting you swap in a 3, 5, or 7-card “core” that grips your cards so they don’t fall out.
Want an ID card, work badge, elastic band for more cards, or a money clip on the end? You can change out the front or back magnetic plates for any of those. Or, change out both for ultra-thin aluminum covers if you don’t need the wallet to magnetically stick to your phone.
You can see it in action in my Today I’m Toying With video embedded in this post (also on YouTube and on Instagram if you prefer).
My favorite part is that the whole kit snaps together using a compliant mechanism — the plastic arms of the card-carrying core act like springs, pushing a little locking mechanism into the notches of each modular cover you add as you slide the parts together. Once your cards are inside, they keep the arms apart so it can’t open accidentally (unless you drop the entire wallet). It’s all very clever.
Even when I did drop the wallet (thanks for the suggestion , hugo!), it didn’t explode, typically. Usually, it just came apart slightly, though I did drop it hard on concrete one time and was able to make a small explosion: one half popped off, and two cards came out, but everything landed in a two-foot radius. The wallet has a big dent now.
There are definitely some downsides. While OhSnap advertises the Wallet 2 as “impossibly thin,” it’s only truly surprisingly sleek in its thinnest 3-card variant, without the thicker and heavier MagSafe and MagStack (which lets you snap other magnets to it) plates attached.
But the reason I’m not buying one is the price and weight. The 7-card version makes my phone feel too heavy, adding 127 grams, and while I happily made the 3-card my wallet for a few weeks, it’d cost me $61 on Kickstarter or $76 retail to get that with a double-magnet kit. OhSnap’s also charging more than I’d like ($35 for an ID cover or a money clip!) for extras .
OhSnap didn’t get me this time. But I could see giving one as a present.

articles.title_orig: Detecting deepfakes, in a world where even reality is suspect
articles.title_zh: Detecting deepfakes, in a world where even reality is suspect
articles.content_orig:
Last February, a Tomahawk cruise missile struck an Iranian elementary school, killing more than 150 people, most of them children. President Trump initially suggested that it could have been somebody else's Tomahawk: "Whether it's Iran or somebody else, the fact that a Tomahawk – a Tomahawk is very generic, it's sold to other countries, but that's being investigated right now," he said.
When Iran put out video as evidence that it was a U.S. missile, Hany Farid , one of the world's foremost experts on deepfakes, was contacted by several media outlets to determine if it was real or fake.
A professor at Dartmouth College, Farid is also co-founder of GetReal Security , a cyber security firm. "What was difficult about this case was you had very little to work on," he said. "We had a very grainy, shaky video. The missile is extremely small. And we had to reason about the physical plausibility of that missile striking the ground."
But he also had certain aspects that he could study scientifically, involving the speed of sound, the speed of light, and the size of the missile: "And those three things were enough for us to say that this is physically plausible," he said. "And this is the important part: all evidence led us to the belief that the video was authentic, and there's been no refuting of that."
But that's the world we live in: Reality itself, so perfectly mimicked by artificial intelligence, that even reality is suspect.
Farid said, "Here's the thing that makes me a little crazy, as a scientist in particular: I don't think you should be able to go into a court of law and say, 'Here is some evidence that is damning enough to put this person to death,' and then the judge says, 'Well, how do you know it's real?' And I say, 'Well, because the computer told me so.' This is not an answer
"And if I can't explain to you, to a judge, and to a jury, what is happening here – because the lighting, because the shadows, because the geometry, whatever it is – that's what we need to be able to do."
A case in point: Alex Pretti, who was killed by an ICE agent in Minnesota. If you remember the scene last January 24, it was chaotic. Several ICE agents with guns surrounded Pretti.
Farid showed us a blurry photo of Pretti that was taken from the original video. "Somebody took this and 'enhanced' it," he said. According to Farid, the crispness of this "enhanced" image makes the scene feel "more real, but what it also did is when it enhanced it, it seems to have put a gun in [Pretti's] hand. If you go back to this video, the camera's panning a little bit and what's happening is, there's a shadow behind his hand on the street. And what the AI did is that it hallucinated this."
Farid says artificial intelligence has learned, "When you see photos like this with three men with guns, everybody's got a gun." And now, when you do Google searches for events like Pretti's killing, it shows the "enhanced" image.
By Farid's estimate, half of the content that's widely viewed on the Internet is fake, basically a toss of the coin. Much of it has its own sneering label: "AI slop." Footage of airplanes skidding on the tarmac, toddlers dancing a two-step, Elvis. "AI slop is a broad term that defines people generating content using AI just to grab eyeballs, video after video after video driving engagement," Farid said.
For the most part, Farid limits his examinations to the really serious stuff, the deepfakes. Even so, he's inundated. He said, "We're seeing deepfakes being weaponized in many, many different ways, from the creation of child sexual abuse material, to non-consensual intimate imagery, to full-blown state-sponsored disinformation campaigns, to what the North Koreans have done, [which] is to have their IT workers interview for jobs remotely. And they conceal their accent using AI. They can conceal their identity using a deepfake, where they change their identity from eyebrow to chin, cheek to cheek, in real time over a video call. They can conceal their geolocation. And they interview for jobs. I will tell you, just about every single Fortune 500 company has hired one or more of these, whether they know it or not.
"And now, the question you want to ask yourself is, what's next? Well, so one CEO said, 'Okay. No more virtual interviews. No more remote work.' That's insane. … We're gonna start flying people across the country? That can't be the answer. I mean it's exhausting. Let's be honest. I mean, if we're always looking at our shoulder over every email, every text message, every voicemail, every phone call, every video call? It's exhausting. I'm exhausted, and I do this for a living."
Asked if he has nightmares over deepfakes, Farid replied, "I look at content all day long. And usually the things I look at are not pleasant. I'm looking at bad things that involve horrific crimes, and when you view these things over and over and over again, they sit with you and you can't get them out of your head.
'And number two is, I don't want to be wrong. And five years ago I felt a lot more confident about our ability to distinguish real from fake. It's gotten harder. And then I worry more. I feel like the ground is constantly shifting," he said.
It builds – the stress, the pressure. After seven years on the West Coast, Farid returned to Dartmouth College, where he had previously spent 20 years on faculty. His wife, Emily Cooper, is also a professor there. The two of them bought a rural property in neighboring Vermont, where Farid mows acres of meadows, and cuts enough wood to feed their stoves through the winter. It's enough mowing and cutting to rinse some of those disturbing images away. It's isolated – there's no mail delivery, no garbage pickup –  but it's peaceful.
Certain work-related issues linger. Social media? Farid loathes it: "You can look at social media, at online platforms and say there is measurable harm coming to young kids, to adults, to seniors, across the boards. And I think we have been so mesmerized by these products which are, by design, meant to be addictive.
"I think we did an experiment on an entire generation of these young kids coming up, putting these devices in their hands. And now we've woken up and we're like, 'Oh, my God. This is terrible.' This generation right now has lower learning outcomes than any generation in history. Go to Palo Alto at the fanciest private schools where all the tech billionaires send their kids. There's no devices in those classrooms. They know."
That $17 billion settlement that Meta reached a few weeks back includes some safeguards, like a two-hour time limit for users under the age of 18. Farid thinks that's a start, but not nearly enough.
"The darkest vision I have is that everybody lives in their own information ecosystem, and nobody knows how to talk to each other anymore," he said.
On platforms where algorithms prefer fake to real content, Farid thinks all of us should stay off social media, or at the very least take those apps off our phones, to resist the temptation. As for those websites that promise to detect AI fakes, he says it's not that simple: "Here's what I think is next (and by saying next, I mean in the coming year), which is most of the deepfakes that we are seeing today have a human somewhere in the process. Somebody's hands are on the keyboard. There's still a human in the loop. But what's gonna start happening is AI agents are gonna start creating their own fakes."
And what is an AI agent? "An agent just has more autonomy, and what we have started to see is when you give it a problem to solve, it will find creative ways to do it, including creating a fake identity to interact with a human to get a human to do something and then it will lie about it," he said.
AI agents have been in the news recently for going rogue in testing trials, intensifying the global debate over AI safety and the very course of humanity . These are issues Hany Farid grapples with every day.

articles.title_orig: This NYC startup requires 4 days in office but just let everyone work remote for a whole month
articles.title_zh: This NYC startup requires 4 days in office but just let everyone work remote for a whole month
articles.content_orig:
Bruno Solari spent his August traveling all around Spain, starting with a week in Ibiza, continuing on to Madrid, Málaga, Marbella and Barcelona, before finally returning to Ibiza for a bachelor party.
He also managed to squeeze in a few meetings and client calls all throughout.
Solari, founder and CEO of the New York City-based PR firm SolComms, was among his company's 53 employees enjoying their inaugural "Work from Anywhere August." Other employees logged on from all over the U.S. (the Jersey Shore, the Hamptons, Florida) and the world (Berlin, Prague, London, Portugal).
"I was in Spain the entire month of August, and I would have felt like a hypocrite if I was going to be there and making my team be in-office," Solari, 33, tells CNBC Make It. "So I thought, 'OK, I'm doing this myself. I'm going to grant that flexibility to the entire agency.'"
The end-of-summer experiment felt like a worthwhile risk to the 3-year-old startup: Employee surveys of the trial indicate boosted productivity, work-life balance and happiness, while the business also saw a modest revenue boost. It also runs counter to several big companies scaling back on remote-work flexibility in a job market where employers have the upper hand.
"I think people were surprised that I went for it," Solari says.
Four weeks of fully remote work from anywhere in the world is a bold move for the millennial founder, who came up in PR agencies at the height of the hustle culture era and says he holds more "traditional" workplace values, like building company culture through in-person interactions rather than "through a screen" of fully remote work. Since its founding in 2023, SolComms has operated with a four days in-office requirement, with Fridays at home that end at 3 p.m. most weeks (and 12 p.m. during the summer).
Some 25% of full-time U.S. workers work in a hybrid arrangement, with the most common requirements being three days in the office, followed by four, according to a recent report from Owl Labs , a video-conferencing technology company, which surveyed 2,000 people in July. Most, 65%, work onsite full time, and 10% work remotely full time.
Solari says every year his company surveys its own employees about the perks and benefits they want, and every year they ask for more work-from-home days. Wary of granting another remote working day during the week, Solari thought to offer 100% flexibility within a one-month period instead.
He and his leadership team came up with the idea in January, announced it to employees in February, and spent the next six months coming up with best practices to make sure everyone was set up for remote success.
Among those guidelines: Stick to 9 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. EST working hours, keep cameras on for all meetings, dress for meetings as if you were going into the office, use Slack status updates liberally, take lunch and other breaks, and no sensitive calls or screens in public spaces.
SolComms also communicated their remote-August plans to the agency's 80-plus clients across healthcare, tech and AI, and consumer brands, says Natalie Valicenti, 30, the company's associate vice president of operations, who split her remote month across Rhode Island and Minnesota.
The SolComms benefit comes at a time when many company leaders are scaling back on employee flexibility and benefits, and during a tightening labor market where employers have the upper-hand.
In September, Uber announced plans to cut about 3,300 corporate jobs, as well as scale down its remote workforce and tighten in-office rules. Disney said it would require more employees to report to the office four days a week and later announced layoffs of about 300 employees.
The five-day return-to-office creep has been growing for several years. The share of Fortune 500 companies requiring five days in the office nearly doubled from mid-2024 to mid-2025, from 13% to 24%, according to research from Flex Index , a resource within the advisory firm Work Forward that analyzes office requirements data.
But for SolComms, the risks of loosening office requirements for a month seem to have paid off.
Twenty-one employees answered a survey following the inaugural remote month, with 76% saying they were more productive, 90% saying they maintained high work-life balance, and 100% saying they want Work from Anywhere August back next year, according to documents reviewed by Make It. Several say the experience helped them strengthen their communication and self-management skills, and a lot of people said cutting their commute times was the biggest draw.
There were also some downsides, like staffers saying they felt tied to their computers and found it hard to step away, whereas it felt more natural to take breaks for lunch, coffee or a walk if they were in the office.
Solari says he sees this "internal pressure to be available" as a common struggle with remote work.
"I think it's a matter of continuing to let employees know that we're flexible," he says. "You don't need to be chained to a desk to prove that you're doing a good job, and ultimately, it's not always the person who's the first to respond who's the power player in producing results."
Though not the goal, Solari says, the business also saw financial benefits: Revenue increased by a modest 4% revenue from July to August, and jumped 12% from August to September.
Solari is already committed to a return of the program in August 2027.
"[We're] 1,000% doing it again, without a doubt," he says.

articles.title_orig: WRC: Elfyn Evans becomes world champion after late Oliver Solberg crash
articles.title_zh: WRC: Elfyn Evans becomes world champion after late Oliver Solberg crash
articles.content_orig:
Elfyn Evans and co-driver Scott Martin won just two of 13 races in the 2026 WRC season
Elfyn Evans became Britain's first world rally champion for 25 years after rival Oliver Solberg crashed in a highly dramatic finish to the season in Italy.
Sweden's Solberg was on course to snatch the lead on the final stage of the last round of the World Rally Championship, and thereby deny Evans the title.
But Solberg lost control of his car with a few hundred metres to go in the Rally Italia Sardegna, which meant the glory went to Welshman Evans, a five-time runner-up in the championship.
"It hasn't sunk in," said a shocked Evans.
"I was sure it was over. I feel for Oliver - he had an incredible weekend. I don't know what to say."
The 37-year-old and co-driver Scott Martin had led for much of the 2026 season and took a 21-point advantage into the final round in Sardinia.
But that gap had shrunk to a solitary point by the time the drivers lined up for the last of 17 stages, bringing back painful memories of previous narrow misses for Evans.
Solberg, 25, needed only to beat his Toyota team-mate in the final stage to claim enough bonuses to be champion, but he crashed two corners from the finish.
Evans becomes only the third British man to win the WRC title after Colin McRae in 1995 and Richard Burns in 2001.
World champion Evans reflects on 'incredible finish'
Relive dramatic final stage shootout for title as it happened
The five titles that got away as Evans seeks WRC glory
Solberg, whose father Petter won the WRC title in 2003, won the rally by almost a minute ahead of nine-time world champion Sebastien Ogier.
With barely a kilometre to run of the final stage he and English co-driver Elliott Edmondson were 1.9 seconds up on Evans and closing at speed on the championship.
Though Solberg got back on the road, his crash meant he finished nine seconds slower than his team-mate - and five points behind Evans in the overall standings.
A third Toyota driver, Sami Pajari, finished a further one point behind in third - having seen his own title challenge evaporate on the final weekend.
An inconsolable Solberg remained in his car for some time at the end of the stage before being encouraged to take to the podium by Gazoo Racing team principal Jari-Matti Latvala and team-mate Ogier.
"Two corners, two corners," said an emotional Solberg.
"First congratulations to Elfyn, he has been very consistent all season. That I even had a shot after my rollercoaster of a season is incredible.
"I tried everything. I knew I was pushing but didn't know if it was enough. I pushed even more and I couldn't save the car. I tried my very best."
Evans, from Dolgellau in north Wales, had previously missed out on the title on the final day three times and in two of those seasons he had taken a lead into the concluding rally before losing out to Ogier in 2020 and 2025.
"I don't really know what my reaction is. It's surreal with how it happened. It's a relief," he said.
"It wouldn't by my proudest way of winning it, but it's job done."
For Toyota sporting director Kaj Lindstrom there were mixed feelings.
"That was the hardest thing. The ending was quite something, I didn't expect it," said the Finn.
"It was a good fight and we all saw that Oliver was all or nothing. It held all the way to the end.
"Oliver still has time but Elfyn finally got his title so we're really happy for him."
Jon Armstrong was competing in his first full season at the top level in the World Rally Championship
The WRC season was reduced to 13 rounds when the Saudi Arabia event, originally planned for next month, was cancelled because of the ongoing unrest in the Middle East.
Rally Italia Sardegna marked the end of Jon Armstrong's rookie season at the top level of WRC, and he produced his best result when finishing seventh.
"It's been good to have a clean weekend with a strong result," said the M-Sport Ford driver.
"It's not been an easy year and this was a rally to show we can put it together. A big thanks to everyone who has been supporting us, it's been a great year and it's been a privilege to drive this car."
Armstrong's team-mate and fellow Irishman Josh McErlean did not fare as well despite running as high as sixth on Saturday before retiring after a collision with a tree.
He also had to stop twice on Sunday before finishing well off the pace but claimed ninth spot in the championship.
