articles.title_orig: U.S. Coast Guard locates debris from missing plane off Nantucket, search for missing passengers ongoing
articles.title_zh: U.S. Coast Guard locates debris from missing plane off Nantucket, search for missing passengers ongoing
articles.content_orig:
The Coast Guard located debris that was confirmed to be associated with the missing aircraft off Nantucket, the U.S. Coast Guard told NewsCenter 5 on Saturday.
The search is still ongoing for the six missing passengers who were on board, the Coast Guard said.
The Gulfstream G-100 aircraft departed L.F. Wade International Airport in Bermuda and was traveling to Boston's Logan International Airport.
A Massport spokesperson confirmed that the aircraft did not arrive at Logan Airport as scheduled.
The Bermuda government said it has been in contact with the families of those on board.
“My thoughts are with everyone on board and their families during this deeply worrying time," said Premier David Burt. "We are praying that all six people will be found safe, and we thank the search and rescue crews for their continuing efforts.”
In a statement from Skyport, the company that manages Wade International Airport, a spokesperson said that the aircraft was a Canadian-registered air ambulance that left its airport for Boston at 12:41 a.m. on Saturday.
The company said there were four crew members and two passengers on board. The passengers were traveling to Boston for medical care.
"The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has advised that air traffic controllers subsequently lost contact with the aircraft off the coast of Nantucket Island, Massachusetts, and a search is currently underway," the spokesperson said. "Skyport has no further information to provide at this time."
The Federal Aviation Administration said it issued a search and rescue alert for the plane at 1:20 a.m.
The FAA notified the U.S. Coast Guard that it lost contact with the plane, which is registered to Canadian-based Latitude Air Ambulance. The company confirmed that the missing plane is among its fleet. The Coast Guard's response includes crews from Air Station Cape Cod, a 47-foot motor lifeboat crew from Station Brant Point and the USCGC William Sparling -- a fast response cutter.
The search is about 13 nautical miles off the coast and extends from about 30 nautical miles wide and 20 nautical miles long, according to the Coast Guard.
WCVB will have more information when it becomes available.

articles.title_orig: Bernie Sanders makes a late push for California billionaire tax
articles.title_zh: Bernie Sanders makes a late push for California billionaire tax
articles.content_orig:
Google cofounder Sergey Brin has now spent more than nine figures combating California’s proposed wealth tax.
According to filings , Brin donated a total of $102 million to the group Building a Better California, a PAC and political advocacy organization opposing the state’s billionaire tax and supporting other pro-business policies and housing and infrastructure affordability. Campaign filings show efforts to block this tax have exceeding $187 million, making Brin the largest sole contributor to the effort. Contributions supporting the bill have meanwhile reached about $32 million.
Proposition 40 , which will be on the ballot in November, would impose a one-time, 5% tax on California’s 200 billionaires, with 90% of the revenue from the proposed measure going toward the state’s health care program and 10% going toward education, food assistance, and administration. Brin, with a net worth of nearly $260 billion , could owe about $13 billion as a result of the tax.
California, the most populous state, has become the epicenter of the conversation around the K-shaped economy, or the diverging fortunes of those with wealth and those without it. While the Golden State has a $4 trillion GDP, making its economy about the same size as the United Kingdom’s, it also has 18% of its residents living below the poverty line , the highest in the country, in part because of its high cost of living.
The ballot measure has caused an uproar among some of California’s wealthiest individuals such as former Google CEO Eric Schmidt and PayPal cofounder Peter Thiel, both of whom have donated to organizations against the measure. Brin compared the proposal to his socialist Soviet upbringing.
“I fled socialism with my family in 1979 and know the devastating, oppressive society it created in the Soviet Union. I don’t want California to end up in the same place,” he told the New York Times in a statement in April.
California Gov. Gavin Newsom has joined these tech billionaires in combating the measure, arguing the tax would hurt the state by eroding its tax base, ultimately reducing key revenue for social services.
“The fact is it actually will reduce investments in education,” Newsom said in a Bloomberg Businessweek interview earlier this year. “It will reduce investments in teachers and librarians, childcare. It will reduce investments in firefighting and police.”
The opposition to Prop 40 may, in some ways, be a self-fulfilling prophecy, as billionaires including Brin shift business entities out of California in favor of states without similar wealth taxes. Brin now lists Nevada as his residence, according to state records. Larry Page, who cofounded Google alongside Brin, has converted several of his assets out of California, including Koop, his family office, which was incorporated in Delaware in December 2025. Oceankind, an ocean science nonprofit founded by Page’s wife, Lucy Southworth, in 2018 , was similarly incorporated in Delaware around the same time. Brin, for his own part, reportedly bought a $51 million home near Miami Beach in March.
There’s not yet clear evidence to indicate these billionaires’ anxieties about the future of California are well-founded. On one hand, the six billionaires expected to leave California—Brin, Page, Thiel, as well as car loan magnate Don Hankey, former Uber CEO Travis Kalanick, and director Steven Spielberg—would have collectively generated about $27 billion in tax revenue, about one-fourth of the $100 billion the proposal is expected to raise through taxes over five years.
On the other hand, billionaires were already paying so little in California income tax their departure may not pack as much of a punch as anticipated. A working paper published by the National Bureau of Economic Research in May noted billionaires residing in the state paid $4.1 billion in income tax last year, about 0.2% of their collective $2 trillion net worth, meaning that even if every billionaire were to leave the state, it would take about 25 years for lost income tax revenue to cancel out the $100 billion sum California is projected to get from the tax. Even if a billionaire mass exodus included one-quarter of the state’s wealthiest residents, it would take a century to equal the $100 billion windfall.
“The proposed one-off California billionaire tax of 5%, payable over five years, is both small relative to California billionaires’ wealth gains and large relative to the taxes they currently pay,” the authors wrote.
A version of this story was published on Fortune.com on Aug. 11, 2026.

articles.title_orig: Trump defends data centers in Ohio, warns they’ll go to China if US turns them away
articles.title_zh: Trump defends data centers in Ohio, warns they’ll go to China if US turns them away
articles.content_orig:
President Trump defended the rapid buildout of massive data centers Saturday as he rallied supporters in Ohio to turn out for Republican candidates in next month’s midterm elections — warning that blocking the tech projects would hand an advantage to China.
“There’s so much money to be made for Ohio. You can’t just turn them off. They’ll go to China,” Trump told supporters at the campaign rally outside Dayton — where he urged voters to back Republican Sen. Jon Husted and gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy.
Trump repeatedly told the crowd in the battleground state to act as though he himself were on the ballot in the November 3 midterms.
“Please pretend that I’m on the ballot, and you need to turn out for a midterm victory,” he said.
Trump said his administration was taking “historic action” to make sure large technology companies behind data centers benefit surrounding communities.
The president tied the data center boom to the global race over artificial intelligence, saying the US was ahead of China in what he repeatedly called “superintelligence.”
Trump said China “doesn’t want to see us,” adding, “We’re beating China” in the technology race as he argued against turning data centers away from the US.
At the same time, Trump backed legislation pushed by Husted that he said would “stop data centers from raising electricity costs and require them to pay their own way.”
Trump said nearly every Senate Democrat had voted days earlier to block the measure.
He vowed to sign the Ratepayer Protection Act “into law immediately within 24 hours” if Republicans prevailed.
The surge in data center development has triggered a bipartisan backlash across the country as communities grapple with the enormous amounts of electricity, water and land required to power the facilities.
The biggest fight has centered on who should pay for the infrastructure needed to serve the projects.
Utilities may need to build new power plants, substations and transmission lines for massive data center loads, raising concerns that households and other businesses could be stuck with higher bills if those costs are spread across the broader rate base.
Water use, noise and sprawling footprints have also fueled resistance, particularly in areas where projects sit near homes or rely on strained water supplies.
Critics have also questioned generous state and local tax breaks for facilities that can cost billions of dollars to build but employ relatively few workers once construction is finished.
The political pressure has prompted officials in several states to rethink the incentives and fast-track approvals once used to lure the industry.
Some states have paused tax breaks or permitting, while others have pushed special utility rates and requirements aimed at making developers shoulder more of the cost of serving their facilities.
Trump was in Ohio after stops in Texas, Oklahoma and Alabama this week as part of what he says will be a 32-day jaunt ahead of the midterms.

articles.content_orig:
Outsourcing life’s mundane tasks buys us freedom, but risks relinquishing the experience of living, says online observer
From cooking and attending hospital visits to doing the actual quarrelling, paid “life stand-ins” are stepping in to manage these tasks, along with errands and awkward moments that many young Chinese would rather avoid.
This trend, known as the “stand-in economy,” is gaining traction among time-strapped consumers who are willing to pay for convenience when daily responsibilities exceed their time, patience, or expertise.
First widely reported by mainland media in 2024, the movement has since blossomed into a vast market for highly personalised errand services.
On RedNote, posts about paid handicraft and assembly assistance have garnered over 120 million views. For example, some users buy intricate Lego sets but lack the time needed to assemble them, opting instead to hire professional builders.

articles.title_orig: France’s violent student protests raise warning for America: ‘A cautionary tale’
articles.title_zh: France’s violent student protests raise warning for America: ‘A cautionary tale’
articles.content_orig:
‘The Big Weekend Show’ panel discusses protests in France over complaints about teacher shortages, school days and deteriorating facilities.
France’s violent student protests are fueling fresh warnings about the consequences of open-border immigration policies, with the unrest being held up as a "cautionary tale" for the U.S.
"I would also say as we’re sitting here in beautiful New York City, this is a cautionary tale," "The Big Weekend Show" co-host Tomi Lahren said Saturday.
She continued: "This is something we’re learning from Europe, and we would be wise to learn from Europe. They decided they wanted to have open borders. They decided they wanted diversity as their strength, and of course, Joe Biden tried that for four years. We’re undoing that currently."
FRANCE'S TEEN RIOTS TAKE EXPLOSIVE NEW TURN AS GOVERNMENT POINTS FINGER AT HARD LEFT
Policemen stand in front of burning garbage as they face students during a protest against under-resourced schools in Paris on Friday. (Aurelien Morissard/AP Photo)
Lahren posited that "when you let so many people come into your country, leech off of your system, then the people who are from there are going to at some point get upset."
She said that anger often becomes misplaced and, "they end up lighting things on fire, which I think is stupid no matter what you’re angry with, but it’s no doubt these countries that say we’re going to be a global home for everybody, they end up paying the price, and it’s usually the native Frenchmen, or whenever they are that end up paying the highest price."
Students in Paris began to protest late last month against what they deemed as overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages, long school days and deteriorating conditions, blaming the government for not investing enough in education.
REPUBLICAN GLEE ERUPTS AS WHITE HOUSE BOASTS SHARP DECLINE IN IMMIGRATION FROM MUSLIM-MAJORITY NATIONS
A student kicks a tear gas canister during a protest against under-resourced schools in Paris on Friday. (Aurelien Morissard/AP Photo)
The demonstrations started peacefully in Paris’ poorer suburbs but quickly spread to Paris itself, then went nationwide in cities like Marseille, Strasbourg, Tours, Nantes, Toulouse ​and Lille, becoming increasingly violent as they expanded.
The protests were also fueled by the government’s 2027 budget unveiling on Thursday, which showed education spending would rise by only 1.7%, excluding teacher pensions, an increase which is below the rate of inflation, Reuters reported.
Rioters have committed arson, vandalism, thrown objects at police and even assaulted people in some cases, prompting authorities to respond with tear gas and rubber bullets.
TENS OF THOUSANDS FLOOD STREETS TO PROTEST SPAIN BORDER CRISIS
Students block the entrance of Voltaire high school in Paris as they protest against under-resourced schools on Friday. (Aurelien Morissard/AP Photo)
More than 5,000 protesters were arrested this week across the country, according to Reuters, and more than 400 schools remained closed as of Friday.
Euronews reported Friday that at least 65 school staff members, including 40 principals, have been injured since the unrest began, along with roughly 170 students.
More than 100 high schools have suffered what Education Minister Édouard Geffray described as "severe damage."
French intelligence agencies told a government crisis meeting Thursday that the protest movement had been initiated by politicians from the hard-left France Unbowed Party, known as LFI, Reuters reported Friday.
LIZ PEEK: ANGRY, AFFLUENT AND ADRIFT — WHAT'S DRIVING SOME YOUNG AMERICANS TO VIOLENCE
Anti-riot police officers face protesting students carrying out blockading action outside the secondary school Le Corbusier, in Aubervilliers, northern Paris on Friday. (Lou Benoist / AFP via Getty Images)
LFI has denied the allegations and accused President Emmanuel Macron 's government of politicizing the protests ahead of France's 2027 presidential election.
Simone Rodan-Benzaquen, senior envoy to Europe at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, told Fox News Digital on Thursday that the unrest began with legitimate concerns but has since evolved into something far more serious.

"The students’ grievances about missing teachers and deteriorating schools were real at first," Rodan-Benzaquen said. "But dousing a principal in gasoline and attacking firefighters are acts of extreme violence. What makes this politically significant is the effort to turn frustration over schools into a much broader confrontation with the government."
Fox News' Efrat Lachter contributed to this report.
Brie Stimson is a Los Angeles-based entertainment and breaking news writer for Fox News Digital.

articles.title_orig: Cornell president says university 'must do better' on handling of sexual assault allegations
articles.title_zh: Cornell president says university 'must do better' on handling of sexual assault allegations
articles.content_orig:
Cornell University President Michael I. Kotlikoff said Saturday his school's administration "must do better" amid the criticism and fallout of its investigation into allegations made by a former student that she was gang-raped at a fraternity in 2024.
"I believe we as an administration and we as a community must do better," Kotlikoff said in a video message posted online Saturday. "We must do everything we can to prevent what happened to Jane Doe and everyone before her and anyone after her from ever happening again."
The former student, identified only as Jane Doe, filed a lawsuit last month against the university and seven men, alleging she was drugged and raped in October 2024 at the university's Chi Phi fraternity chapter when she was 20 years old.
"This has been one of the most difficult weeks in our history, and I know many of you are angry, saddened and struggling," Kotlikoff said.
Back in 2024, the Tompkins County district attorney found that "there was insufficient evidence to support criminal charges." No criminal charges have been filed in the case.
However, Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said this week that he was never given the full transcript of Jane Doe's two-day interview with campus police that occurred in November 2024, about three weeks after the incident, but was only presented a six-page sworn statement based on that interview.
Cornell University initially said its police department provided the results of the school's Title IX investigation to the DA. However, in an FAQ published on its website regarding the allegations, the university said in an Oct. 1 update that it "shared the victim's sworn statement and the Snapchat screenshot with the Tompkins County District Attorney's Office, which is the established protocol if the department believes it is possible a crime has occurred."
The Snapchat screenshot refers to a Snapchat group chat that involved members of the Chi Phi fraternity on the night of the alleged rape.
Van Houten said this week he is reopening the investigation, but New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, who has been publicly critical of Van Houten's approach to the case, said she had appointed State Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor to lead the investigation.
Kotlikoff revealed that the school would be hiring an outside law firm to conduct an "independent review" of "all aspects of Cornell's handling of the 2024 matter." The school has said that it supports the state's criminal probe, which Kotlikoff reiterated Saturday.
The school president admitted the situation "raises questions around the investigations conducted after the allegations were reported."
Kotlikoff earlier this week disclosed that the school's Title IX investigation resulted in two of the accused being expelled and two being suspended for at least two semesters. One had already graduated before any punishment could be handed down, Kotlikoff  said, and two were found not to be responsible for sexual misconduct.
"I also hear the frustration that Cornell has not communicated enough about what the university did after the assault was reported, which has led to distrust," Kotlikoff said in his video. "There are real legal and privacy limits on what we can say, but we will make greater effort to explain what we can, to provide context about the actions Cornell has taken, and to be more transparent."
He noted that in 2025, in the wake of the initial investigation into Jane Doe's allegations, the university established the Presidential Task Force on Campus Sexual Assault and endorsed the task force's recommendations.
Kotlikoff said in the coming weeks, the university will create opportunities for community members, including parents of current students, to question and talk to school leadership.
"This is a defining moment in Cornell's history," Kotlikoff said. "We must lead the way. We owe it to Jane Doe and to survivors of assault to get this right. And we must keep each other safe."

articles.title_orig: Cornell University police made drug arrest hours before alleged sexual assault
articles.title_zh: Cornell University police made drug arrest hours before alleged sexual assault
articles.content_orig:
Cornell University police made a drug-related arrest at a fraternity house 22 hours before a former student alleges she was drugged and sexually assaulted there, according to police records.
The Cornell Daily Sun reported Saturday that campus police responded to the Chi Phi fraternity house shortly after 1 a.m. on Oct. 19, 2024, made a drug-related arrest and referred an individual to the university’s Office of Student Conduct.
The archived police log cited by the Sun and reviewed by NBC News does not identify the individual or the drugs involved or establish a connection between the drug incident and the alleged assault later that night.
Cornell University had no comment. Its police department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The former Cornell student, identified as Jane Doe, filed a lawsuit last month against the university and seven Chi Phi brothers, alleging she was sexually assaulted over the course of hours that night while she was under the influence of ketamine, alcohol and marijuana.
In a police interview conducted after the alleged assault and documented in records obtained by NBC News, a woman told investigators she had seen a fraternity member with a bag of ketamine about two months earlier. She also said he had previously overdosed and been transported for treatment. The interview does not establish when that occurred or whether she witnessed it.
Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff said in a video message Saturday afternoon that what Jane Doe alleges is “deeply disturbing” and raised questions about the investigation that followed.
“I believe we as an administration, and we as a community, must do better,” he said.
NBC News reported Friday that Cornell police interviewed witnesses and received anonymous tips in the first weeks of their investigation, but Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten did not review that additional information before deciding not to bring charges.
Van Houten said he based his decision on Jane Doe’s initial six-page statement to police, which he argued did not allege criminality. Her attorney, Thomas Giuffra, has said authorities failed to conduct a thorough investigation and prejudged the events based on her statement that she had consented to parts of the night.
Gov. Kathy Hochul on Thursday appointed New York Attorney General Letitia James as a special prosecutor to consider whether criminal charges are appropriate.
“In what world does the district attorney not even interview her or anyone else involved, or even request the full transcript” of her interview, Hochul asked at a news conference Friday.
I’m a reporter on NBC News’ breaking news team, covering crime, extreme weather, pop culture and more. I recently covered Hurricane Milton, which devastated the Tampa, Florida, metropolitan area, and the student-led protests at Columbia University.
Shayna Jacobs is a national reporter for NBC News digital.

articles.title_orig: Former vendor’s viral post sparks backlash against Kissimmee’s World Food Trucks
articles.title_zh: Former vendor’s viral post sparks backlash against Kissimmee’s World Food Trucks
articles.content_orig:
Nick Neville , Community Correspondent , Orlando, FL
Anthony Guevara , Photojournalist
KISSIMMEE, Fla. – A now former vendor at Kissimmee’s World Food Trucks says she was forced out of the space she rented for about a decade, triggering a viral backlash and calls online for a boycott of the food truck park.
Gabriella Santos, who operated Los Cipotes, posted a video saying she was given just hours to move her food truck after ten years at the location. The post drew millions of views and sparked a heated debate on social media.
Santos told News 6 that her frustration built for years, citing what she describes as safety concerns, rising operating costs, and feeling unsupported.
She also said vendors paid out of pocket for events, absorbed new fees, and saw sales decline as more trucks were added to the park.
“Somebody’s making that extra money, and it’s not us,” Santos said in a Friday interview.
Santos said a lease renewal meeting this week became a boiling point. She claims a manager asked for access to her point-of-sale system, which she believes was framed as a way to determine rent.
“She said wanted access to the POS, and I said ‘Why do you need access to that?’” Santos said. “’Oh it’s because that’s how we’re going to balance how much your rent is going to be.’”
Santos also raised concerns about what she says were new lease terms, including language she interpreted as requiring 60 percent if a renewed lease was later broken.
World Food Trucks publicly disputed that claim, saying in a social media response: “That claim is completely false.”
Santos later clarified during the interview that she was describing her perception of what the changes would mean for her business, not alleging a literal demand for 60 percent of sales.
“I never said that,” she said. “What I said was that they wanted 60 percent of my business because that’s how I feel. That’s my personal feeling of what you’re doing to me. You’re taking my profits.”
She told News 6 she understand the terms to mean the food truck park would have wanted 60 percent of the remainder of the lease agreement.
Santos said after refusing to sign the new lease, she was told to leave by midnight on Thursday. Photos obtained by News 6 show her former spot is now surrounded by tables.
In a statement to News 6, World Food Trucks said in part, “We respect every vendor’s right to share their experience. We also believe disagreements deserve respectful conversation and accurate information. Our vendors pay a fixed weekly rent, rather than a percentage of their food sales, and we remain committed to clear communication with our vendor community.
Our focus is on supporting the more than 100 businesses that make World Food Trucks possible. We invite everyone to visit, meet the people behind the food, and support the local entrepreneurs who have helped build this community.”
Santos said she believes the viral reaction resonated because people see small business owners as vulnerable.
She said she is speaking for other vendors who are too afraid to go public.
“I think people don’t want little people to get bullied,” she said.

articles.title_orig: Latino Dems urge Democratic Governors Association to put money behind Gina Hinojosa as Texas governor's race tightens
articles.title_zh: Latino Dems urge Democratic Governors Association to put money behind Gina Hinojosa as Texas governor's race tightens
articles.content_orig:
Latino Democratic leaders are renewing calls for the Democratic Governors Association to invest more heavily in Texas after a New York Times/Siena College poll showed Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa narrowly leading Republican Gov. Greg Abbott.
The poll released Saturday found Hinojosa ahead of Abbott by three points, a result within the poll's margin of error. It comes as Hinojosa continues to face a huge financial disadvantage against the three-term Republican governor.  Abbott's reelection campaign and his Republican allies are outspending her by roughly 10-to-1.
More than 70 Latino Democratic leaders from across the country sent a letter this week urging the DGA and its chair, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, to invest $10 million in the Texas governor's race . The New York Times first reported on the letter, which CBS News has confirmed.
Beshear, a potential 2028 presidential contender, has been constrained by the DGA's commitments to first protect incumbent Democratic governors seeking reelection, though some of those incumbents are currently in strong positions.
Julián Castro, who served as secretary of housing and urban development in the Obama administration, renewed the push Saturday following the release of the New York Times poll. Castro, the former mayor of San Antonio and a 2020 presidential contender, took to social media to call for the DGA and Beshear to support Hinojosa "in a real way."
"How much more evidence" of Hinojosa's "strength in Texas" will Beshear and the DGA "have to see before they support her in a real way?" Castro wrote. "She can win!"
The renewed pressure comes as Democrats increasingly see the Lone Star state as competitive in the closing weeks of the campaign, even as Hinojosa continues to face a substantial spending disadvantage --- what some Republicans are describing as a "firewall" --- in a state that President Trump won by nearly 14 points in 2024.

articles.title_orig: $300 million smuggling ring sent computer chips to China, DOJ alleges
articles.title_zh: $300 million smuggling ring sent computer chips to China, DOJ alleges
articles.content_orig:
Chips are seen on a notebook's RAM. Photo: Fernando Gutierrez-Juarez/dpa-Zentralbild/dpa (Photo by Fernando Gutierrez-Juarez/picture alliance via Getty Images)
A California man faces federal charges for his role in a smuggling scheme that the Justice Department alleges moved nearly a third of a billion dollars’ worth of goods. The operation, though, was not suspected of moving drugs or counterfeit goods. Instead, the plot allegedly involved high-end computer parts, particularly ones used for artificial intelligence.
The investigation into the high-dollar operation led to the arrest of Greg Lui, the owner of a San Gabriel Valley-based technology company, the Justice Department announced this week. He is accused of smuggling to China more than $300 million worth of high-end computer servers that held U.S.-manufactured graphics processing units (GPUs) and are subject to export controls.
The Justice Department alleges that Lui’s company, Earthmade Computers Inc., would buy the items, which required U.S. Department of Commerce licenses to export to China, and ship them to countries such as Malaysia and Singapore, where no licenses are needed. From there, Lui and his co-conspirators would send them on to China without obtaining the licenses.
RELATED: Trump says he's sending $90 checks to 20 million seniors: What to know
The indictment alleges that two Malaysia-based shipping companies paid Earthmade $176 million in the first 10 months of 2024 alone. Federal prosecutors stated that Lui, 38, knew the technology was not allowed to be shipped to China and that the federal government considers the restrictions a matter of U.S. national security.
Lui has been charged with one count each of conspiracy to violate the Export Control Reform Act and the Export Administration Regulations, conspiracy to commit money laundering, and outbound smuggling. If convicted, he could serve up to 20 years in prison on each of the first two counts and up to 10 years in prison for the smuggling charge.
The Source: Information for this article was taken from the Department of Justice. This story was reported from Orlando.

articles.title_orig: Flu season is coming. What Michigan residents should know about flu, COVID and RSV shots
articles.title_zh: Flu season is coming. What Michigan residents should know about flu, COVID and RSV shots
articles.content_orig:
SEATTLE — There's a bit of a chill in the air, pumpkin spice in your coffee, and children back to school — which means the threat of respiratory viruses like COVID-19, influenza and RSV is looming.
Some respiratory illnesses have arrived already. Seasonal influenza activity is still low at the national level, data from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention show.
But certain flu metrics are inching up – especially in the West . Health officials in Washington state's King County note that since mid-August there has been an increase in people with flu visiting emergency departments in the area.
Vaccines that help prevent illness and reduce the risk of serious infections and hospitalization are now available, and for some people, this is the right time to roll up their sleeves.
Typically, the CDC launches a fall campaign around this time of year, recommending seasonal immunizations such as the flu shot and COVID-19 vaccines. But after sweeping changes to the agency's vaccine advisory committee during the second Trump administration and ongoing lawsuits, the CDC recently posted guidance online to follow last year's recommendations for flu and COVID-19.
Meanwhile, the American Medical Association and the University of Minnesota's Vaccine Integrity Project launched their own independent reviews of this fall's vaccines – including those for flu , COVID and RSV – which was published in September in the medical journal JAMA.
The review papers helped inform 2026-27 respiratory virus immunization recommendations released by several medical groups, including the American Academy of Pediatrics, American Academy of Family Physicians, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists and the Infectious Diseases Society of America.
"For more than 60 years, the United States has benefited from an established federal process for evaluating vaccine evidence and translating that science into recommendations for the American public. At the center of that process were the Centers for Disease Control and its Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, the ACIP," Dr. Bruce Gellin, board chair of the Vaccine Integrity Project and professor of medicine at Georgetown University, said at a news briefing.
"Unfortunately today, the federal government is not fulfilling that responsibility in the way that it historically has. But the need for that work has not disappeared. Influenza, SARS-CoV-2 and the RSV viruses will circulate again this fall and winter," Gellin said.
"Clinicians will still have patients to care for. Parents will still have decisions to make for their children, and older Americans, pregnant women and people with underlying health conditions will still need to know how best to protect themselves," he said. "We cannot allow the breakdown of a federal process to create a vacuum in evidence-based vaccine guidance."
The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services has not responded to CNN's request for comment on the groups' recommendations.
Flu, COVID-19 and RSV immunizations are now available at most major pharmacies.
"And really reassuringly, insurers have indicated to the major groups that they will cover these respiratory virus immunizations," Dr. Sarah Nosal, president of the American Academy of Family Physicians, said in a news briefing.
Ordering through Vaccines for Children , the federal program that provides routine immunizations at no cost to children who are uninsured or underinsured or whose families may not otherwise be able to afford them, has also started. About half of U.S. children are eligible for the program.
"Vaccines are one of medicine's greatest success stories. They prevent serious illness, reduce hospitalizations and long-term complications and save lives," Nosal said in a news release. "As federal guidance evolves, the science behind vaccines remains strong. These recommendations are grounded in the latest evidence, informed by public health experts and shaped by what family physicians are seeing every day in their patients."
Groups eligible for RSV immunizations include older adults, pregnant people and infants.
"People age 50 and older with high-risk conditions, and everyone over 75 years old, should get one dose," Nosal said. "This is not an annual vaccine. If you got one before, you do not need a new one this year. Getting one should protect you throughout the entire season."
During pregnancy, RSV vaccination is recommended in the third trimester, between weeks 32 and 36.
Children younger than 8 months should be immunized against RSV using a monoclonal antibody unless their mother got an RSV vaccination during pregnancy, said Dr. Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics.
And a single dose of RSV vaccine is recommended for adults who have weakened immune systems.
For older adults, RSV vaccinations are typically recommended in late summer and early fall.
The advice slightly changed this year for pregnant people.
For infants, the RSV monoclonal antibody is typically recommended around virus season, from October through March.
Everyone 6 months and older is recommended to get an annual flu shot.
"On average, flu vaccines reduce the risk of needing to go to the doctor by 30% to 60%," Nosal said.
"Adults 65 years and older should get an enhanced flu vaccine, one that is high-dose, adjuvanted or recombinant, when it's available," she said. "But do not delay your vaccination if that one's not available."
And for the first time, an mRNA-based flu vaccine is available for use in adults 50 and older.
October is the ideal time to get vaccinated, Nolan said, because "protection wanes throughout the season."
Some providers use the slogan "flu before boo" to remind people to get a flu shot before Halloween.
Getting an updated COVID-19 vaccine is recommended for all adults.
"If you're older than 19, we recommend getting the COVID-19 vaccine," Nosal said.
"This is especially important for people who are 65 years and older, at increased risk for severe COVID infection and those who've never received a COVID-19 vaccine," she said. "For those adults 65 years and older, they should receive a second dose of the updated COVID-19 vaccine six months after that season's initial dose to help maintain protection as immunity wanes over time."
The vaccine is also recommended for infants between six months and 23 months of age, and children in certain high-risk groups or those whose families request vaccination.
It's recommended to get the updated vaccine now, but if you have been recently infected with Covid, experts advise waiting four to six months before getting the vaccine.
The updated COVID-19 vaccine "targets the most recent strain that's been circulating, and so if you want to update your protection, that's the best way to do it," Dr. Sandra Adamson Fryhofer, president-elect of the American Medical Association, said in a news briefing.

articles.title_orig: Hawaii sea arch collapses into Pacific Ocean 550 years after its formation
articles.title_zh: Hawaii sea arch collapses into Pacific Ocean 550 years after its formation
articles.content_orig:
A scenic cliff on the wave-swept coast of Hawaii's Big Island has collapsed, the National Park Service said.
The Holei Sea Arch, located in the Hawaii Volcanoes National Park, was about 90 feet high before it collapsed sometime between Sept. 23 and Sept. 27, possibly when the park was temporarily closed during Hurricane Nolo .
"The exact time of the collapse is unknown and could have occurred when the park was temporarily closed during Tropical Storm Nolo," said the Hawai'i Volcanoes National Park in a social media post.
Nolo — which reached winds of 155 mph — moved past Hawaii's Big Island and brought heavy rain and winds to the state last week. Hawaii Gov. Josh Green said the Trump administration approved an emergency declaration for Hawaii that will provide federal resources and assistance to the state in its recovery from Nolo.
In August, Hawaii was battered by Hurricane Lala, which washed away about 100 homes , triggered landslides and caused widespread power outages as it brushed past Hawaii.
The arch's collapse into the Pacific Ocean was not unexpected, however, it marks "the latest transformation of the park's remote and rugged coastline," the NPS said in a Facebook post.
"This formation is beautiful, but temporary, and has a limited life span," NPS said .
People reacting to the post called it a sign of nature taking its course.
Officials at the park service warned visitors to stay away from the site since it is unstable and presents a serious falling hazard.
"Photos on social media show people entering the closed area near where the sea arch once stood, putting themselves and first responders at great risk of falling and drowning," the NPS said.
The popular tourist site was formed about 550 years ago. The name Holei comes from a small endemic plant in the milkweed family.

articles.title_orig: How can the same El Niño cause drought in one part of the world and floods in another?
articles.title_zh: How can the same El Niño cause drought in one part of the world and floods in another?
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
For decades, scientists have struggled to understand the potential link between global warming and El Niño — and whether human activity is making the already powerful climate phenomenon even more extreme and disruptive.
Evidence of a connection has remained elusive, however, as El Niño  is notoriously variable, making it difficult to distinguish long-term changes from its natural ebb and flow.
But now — as this year’s “super” El Niño gains strength — some researchers say they are getting closer to unraveling the mystery.
A study published recently  in the journal Science examines temperature data from more than 900 years of coral records from the Galápagos and suggests that El Niños have become much stronger since people started warming the planet through fossil fuel emissions.
“Prior to the industrial era, we don’t see evidence for periods where the El Niño system is as strong as it is in the most recent decades,” said Julia Cole, a paleoclimatologist at the University of Michigan and the study’s lead author. The swings between warm and cold conditions that define El Niño “were much stronger in the last 40 to 50 years than they were prior to warming.”
A “super” El Niño is now 95% likely to develop this year as the climate pattern gains dramatic strength in the Pacific Ocean — leaving officials across California and beyond bracing for a wet and potentially destructive winter.
The research arrives as experts and officials warn that the current El Niño, which began forming in June, is shaping up to be the strongest ever experienced by a considerable margin . It is developing faster than the previous historic super El Niños of 1997-98 and 2015-16, and is already on track to far exceed historical temperature thresholds.
On Thursday, the World Meteorological Society issued a new El Niño forecast warning that there is a nearly 100% chance it will continue through February, prolonging its effects.
“El Niño is being supersized before our eyes,” read a statement from United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres. “The science leaves no room for doubt: the planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up. Sea surface temperatures are rising, temperatures keep climbing, and the world is in the danger zone of extreme weather.”
El Niños are periods of temporary warming in the tropical Pacific that develop every two to seven years. When they arrive, they trigger widespread changes in weather and climate around the world, from punishing heat waves to dangerous floods and severe droughts. In Southern California, El Niño is associated with warm and wet conditions.
According to authors of the recent study, modern El Niños are about 36% stronger than they were before the start of the industrial era in the mid-1800s, and show a “striking amplification” of about 16% in the last 40 years. El Niño’s strength is primarily measured by how much warmer the sea surface temperature in the tropical Pacific region is than normal.
To be sure, scientists have not yet conclusively established that humanity’s burning of fossil fuels is increasing or intensifying El Niño.
“This is another piece of evidence in an ongoing scientific debate on the role of climate change in El Niño events,” said Zeke Hausfather, a climate scientist at Berkeley Earth who was not involved in the study. “It won’t necessarily settle it, but it’s more weight on the side of the scale for a detectable climate impact.”
The ramifications of a direct connection would be serious. Not only is El Niño a leading driver of climate and weather hazards, but it also imposes “tremendous economic costs, ecological damages, and human suffering globally,” according to the Science study. That includes droughts, floods, infrastructure damage, coral bleaching, wildfires, and agricultural and health effects.
Notably, the study did not find that climate change is worsening the other half of the El Niño Southern Oscillation system — La Niña. If anything, it is making ENSO’s variability “kind of lopsided,” Cole said, meaning that the change in variability leans toward stronger warm events than cold ones.
Uncovering these mechanisms has been a challenge, she said, in part because very few people live in the remote part of the ocean where El Niño forms, and “nobody was out there sticking a thermometer in the water every week” over the centuries to create a historical record. It wasn’t until scientists started receiving satellite data in the 1980s that a complete picture of El Niño began to emerge.
So Cole and her colleagues turned to the coral.
A rare convergence of a powerful El Niño, super king tides and sea level rise spurred by climate change could menace California with record coastal flooding this winter.
Coral can live for decades or centuries, and they form a skeleton of calcium carbonate layers as they grow, kind of like rings on a tree. By measuring aspects of their chemistry — the ratio of strontium to calcium and the relative abundance of rare and common oxygen isotopes — the researchers could determine the ocean temperature in which the coral grew down to a specific month, Cole said.
That allowed them to chart temperature data from the Galápagos dating back almost 1,000 years. The Galápagos sit right where eastern Pacific El Niño events have some of their strongest effects.
Though they didn’t have coral samples for every year of the last millennium, the data they generated “have this really unequivocal signal in them, and we thought it was really important to get them out there,” Cole said.
The findings may not settle the debate once and for all, but they “definitely” show an increase in El Niño’s variance in the modern era, said Art Miller, an oceanographer at Scripps Institution of Oceanography who was not involved with the study.
He said the findings are consistent with the appearance of several unusually large El Niño events in the last three decades — namely, 1997-98, 2015-16 and the one gaining strength now.
They also align with observable warming in the ocean and atmosphere, which are potentially affecting El Niño’s dynamics, he said. In fact, this year’s El Niño is developing against the backdrop of unusually warm ocean temperatures, including a record-breaking marine heat wave in the Pacific Ocean that is providing a hotter baseline for the system.
“Since the equatorial zone of the ocean in the western Pacific was loaded with heat, it was primed for triggering an El Niño,” Miller said. But the connection is something of a two-way street: Although the heat wave helped instigate El Niño in the spring and summer, El Niño is expected to feed warmth back toward the West Coast as it develops, keeping coastal waters warmer than usual in the fall and winter, he said.
Other researchers were more skeptical about the coral study’s findings. University of Pennsylvania climate scientist Michael Mann noted in a post on Bluesky that other factors, such as volcanic and solar activity, could explain patterns seen in the coral record.
For his part, Hausfather cautioned that there are “pretty big uncertainties when you are working with indirect measurements like coral proxy records,” so comparing historical El Niños with modern ones is inherently hard to do.
What’s more, “even if the authors are correct about the climate change link, that doesn’t mean that every single El Niño event will be a strong one,” he said. “El Niño is still largely driven by natural variability, which means that some individual events will be strong and some weak.”
Cole, the lead researcher, agreed. The findings don’t mean that every El Niño will be stronger than the last in a warming world, she said — nor would that be realistic given how unpredictable El Niño can be.
But even if some are weaker than others, the data indicate they are unlikely to revert to preindustrial levels anytime so

articles.title_orig: Gemini app limiting what models free & AI Plus users can access, AI Pro adding Deep Think
articles.title_zh: Gemini app limiting what models free & AI Plus users can access, AI Pro adding Deep Think
articles.content_orig:
Following the compute-based usage change in May, Google will soon introduce limits on which Gemini models free users and AI Plus subscribers can access.
According to an updated support document this week, Gemini app users without a Google AI subscription will be limited to the (3.5) Flash-Lite model. Starting October 9, users who do not pay for Gemini will no longer be able to access (3.6) Flash or (3.1) Pro.
Meanwhile, AI Plus subscribers will be limited to Flash-Lite and Flash, with Pro no longer available. These $4.99 per month users will “receive an email that explains when these changes will take effect.”
There are no regressions for AI Pro and AI Ultra . Rather, $19.99/month customers will get access to the Deep Think option for “maximum parallel reasoning” that’s currently just on the $99.99 and $199.99/month plans.
Gemini 3.1 Pro with Deep Think on AI Ultra
In October, the Gemini app also looks to be adding new “low,” “medium,” and “high” effort levels “for each available model.”
This will increase the model’s ability to complete tasks and provide more thorough answers to queries, but will also use more of your limit.
At the moment, you can just enable “Extended thinking: Complex problem solving.” The three new effort/thinking levels would match what’s available in Google AI Studio and Antigravity.
It’s not clear where Gemini 4 Argon will fit in. Google announced earlier this week that it’s first coming to AI Ultra subscribers. The company has yet to specify whether Argon will be classified as a Pro model or be part of a new tier above it.

articles.content_orig:
Young Men General President Timothy L. Farnes spoke during the Saturday afternoon session of October 2026 general conference about ministering to others with compassion. The following is a summary of what he said.
“As covenant followers of Jesus Christ, we minister with compassion to whomever God places in our path. We do it because that’s what the Savior did. And we’ve made a covenant to follow Him.”
Through the sacrament, Latter-day Saints witness to Heavenly Father their willingness to take upon themselves the name of Jesus Christ. “That means we choose to see as He sees, feel as He feels and do as He would do. His life should be reflected in ours. It means that when someone encounters us, they should experience something of Jesus Christ — His kindness, His patience, His hope, His love, His compassion.”
The Lord promises the Saints will have His Spirit with them; with the gift, they can minister as the Savior would, with His power and His loving kindness.
Connecting with God’s children is a way to stay connected to Him. “Often this happens when God places someone in our path and we have eyes to see them. I call these ‘divine appointments’ …
“Let us pray every day for eyes to see the divine appointments God places before us. Let us put compassion into action and minister to the person in front of us. It’s what Jesus did.”

articles.title_zh: RuneScape 4, The Next MMO From Jagex, Announced At RuneFest This Weekend
articles.content_orig:
Lyrical Animation is developing a new animation series based on “ RuneScape ” in partnership with creator Charlie “MoistCr1TiKaL” White and game developer Jagex, the company’s CEO Jon Bellamy announced on stage at RuneFest in Birmingham, UK, on Saturday.
The project will bring the world of Gielinor to the screen, and marks a new step in Jagex’s ambition to expand the “RuneScape” world beyond the gaming ecosystem.
“For 25 years, our players have helped shape ‘RuneScape’s’ extraordinary world, its characters and its stories,” said Bellamy. “When we talk about the future of ‘RuneScape,’ we don’t just mean games. We see huge potential to bring Gielinor to life in new ways, both for the millions who already know and love it and for a whole new audience. It’s early days, but we’re excited to explore that potential with Charlie and the team at Lyrical Animation, and we wanted our players to be the first to know.”
Jagex first released “RuneScape” in 2001, and it has grown into a massively popular fantasy multiplayer online role-playing game. Through quests, combat, exploration and cooperative adventures, players can forge their own paths through the medieval fantasy world of Gielinor. The franchise now includes “RuneScape,” “Old School RuneScape” and “ RuneScape Dragonwilds .”
White is a longtime member of the “RuneScape” community and has amassed more than 25 million followers across his channels and platforms. “I’ve been playing RuneScape for 22 years, and it’s one of my favorite IPs ever,” said White. “I’m so excited to be working with the team on this project.”
“RuneScape has such a unique storytelling voice, at once laugh-out-loud funny and effortlessly insightful,” said Daniel Dominguez, creative director of Lyrical Animation. “To be allowed to help bring that to life for its millions of fans alongside our dear friend Charlie again is a dream come true.”
Lyrical Animation will produce the project alongside White’s Meatier Productions. Development is in its early stages, and the company expects to reveal more details in 2027.

articles.title_orig: Paramount Debt Drop Spells Trouble for Borrowers: Credit Weekly
articles.title_zh: Paramount Debt Drop Spells Trouble for Borrowers: Credit Weekly
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
(Bloomberg) -- As Paramount Skydance Corp. and Oracle Corp. vault into the ranks of corporate America's biggest borrowers, their links to the same man — billionaire Larry Ellison — are starting to stir angst on Wall Street.
Rodman Joins Trump as He Eyes Meeting With North Korea's Kim
Manchester City Verdict Strains UK-UAE Diplomatic Relations
Health Insurers Ditch Medicare Advantage Plans to Boost Profit
Apple Is Finally Ready to Enter Its Next Big Category: the Smart Home
Angry Bondholders Flood Wall Street With Complaints on Paramount Losses
The assumption among many investors has been that Ellison would step in to support Paramount if it got in financial trouble after taking on $52 billion of additional debt this week to help pay for its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery Inc. But with much of the Ellison family's wealth tied to Oracle shares as the company undertakes its own capital intensive AI buildout, the worry is the value of that safety net could come under pressure just when Paramount needs it most.
Those concerns are already being reflected in the market, money managers say. The cost to insure the debt of both companies against default has converged and is increasingly moving in lock-step, a sign investors are beginning to treat the two credits as intertwined. It's another factor lenders need to consider when assessing the mounting debt and execution risk of the firms, according to Campe Goodman, a portfolio manager at Wellington Management Co.
"You have to consider your total Larry Ellison risk," Goodman said, adding that investors should regard Oracle and Paramount as related bets rather than completely separate credits. "You probably want to consider your exposure to both."
Representatives for Paramount and Oracle didn't respond to requests for comment. Attempts to reach Ellison through his foundation also went unanswered.
Ellison, 82, is backstopping Paramount's takeover of Warner Bros., spearheaded by his son David, via a family trust that guaranteed a significant portion of the roughly $47 billion of equity financing for the deal.
Yet his support also extends beyond the acquisition itself. As Paramount worked to reassure ratings firms about the debt burden the combined company would carry, the Ellison family pledged to take all necessary steps to help bring leverage down in the coming years — a commitment that credit graders and investors viewed as a tacit promise to inject additional capital if needed.
That makes Ellison's ability to follow through on the pledge a key consideration for debtholders.
Just a year ago Oracle's shares soared to a record amid surging AI optimism, briefly making him the world's richest person.
Since then, his fortune has plummeted by almost $200 billion — more than any other person on the globe, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.
To be clear, he's still worth roughly $192 billion, enough to place him among the 10 richest people. But the sharp reversal shows how drastically his fortune can gyrate based on Oracle's stock price.
Last month, Ellison canceled a plan to sell billions of dollars worth of stock in the company, in which he still owns a roughly 40% stake. He also disclosed he had increased the number of shares pledged as collateral for his personal loans.
"The businesses couldn't be more different, but the market is starting to connect them through a common sponsor," said Steven Schweitzer, a portfolio manager at Advent Capital Management. "Part of the Paramount credit story is tied to confidence in the Oracle story, because Larry Ellison's financial strength sits behind both."
Paramount's financing package, which wrapped up Wednesday, included $30 billion of US dollar investment-grade bonds, $12.4 billion-equivalent of junk bonds and $9.46 billion of loans. In conversations ahead of the sale, investors considering whether to buy in were actively discussing how much weight to put on the Ellison family's pledge, according to market participants.
"The issue is if Paramount's not doing well and Oracle stock drops a lot, then you still have the same asset base, and that's where there is potential linkage," said Jawad Hussain, an analyst at S&P Global Ratings. That could leave the market asking, "'could it impact the Ellisons' ability to support the Paramount asset,' which needs to de-lever."
Oracle, for its part, has nearly doubled its long-term debt to more than $160 billion over the past two years, as the company refashions itself as a provider of computing power for artificial intelligence work. It now ranks as the fifth-largest borrower in the US corporate bond market, according to Bloomberg index data.
S&P in July cut Oracle to BBB-, the lowest investment-grade rating, as heavy spending pushed free cash flow deeply into negative territory. Last month it lowered Paramount's issuer credit rating to BB, two notches into junk, on expectations for increased leverage following the Warner Bros. acquisition.
Oracle's debt-fueled spending surge has spooked equity investors, too, overshadowing robust growth in its cloud-computing division and driving a more than 50% decline in its share price over the past year.
Brett Kozlowski, a portfolio manager at GW&K Investment Management, said that the risk cuts both ways for Paramount and Oracle debtholders.
"There is risk to Oracle debt that if the Paramount/WBD merger isn't executed as planned, the Ellison family backstop may link the two credits more than is priced," he said via email. "This creates the potential of convergence between the two credits and benefits Paramount over Oracle as the weaker Paramount debt would get the potential support of the stronger Oracle balance sheet."
--With assistance from Anders Melin and David Scheer.

articles.title_orig: Florida’s dengue outbreak reportedly largest US has seen in decades
articles.title_zh: Florida’s dengue outbreak reportedly largest US has seen in decades
articles.content_orig:
CDC says 392 cases of Dengue were reported for the year so far in the state, along with different county-level data
Several Florida counties recently declared a state of local emergency in response to a spate of dengue fever infections.
Hillsborough county, Florida , officials made the declaration on 24 September as health authorities recorded 134 confirmed cases of dengue fever, which is a mosquito-borne sickness typically found in countries outside the US. Officials said that the spread of the illness poses “an immediate and widespread threat to the public health, safety, and welfare of the residents and visitors of Hillsborough county”.
Controlling the tropical disease – often referred to as breakbone fever because it can cause extreme pain – requires “immediate, aggressive, and continuous” measures such as pesticide application, public education and emergency resource planning, officials said.
Dengue cases have become more common in parts of the US. In 2023, Long Beach and Pasadena reported the first ever known locally acquired cases in California.
The spread of dengue mosquitoes outside tropical and subtropical locales has even hit England, with authorities recently announcing that Aedes aegypti had been found in east London homes.
Scientists have said that global warming is poised to intensify climate-related diseases.
Declaring a local state of emergency enables Hillsborough county – whose seat is the city of Tampa – to request “any available and necessary state, federal, and local emergency funds, grants, financial assistance, and mutual aid” in their ongoing fight against mosquitoes carrying dengue. The initial declaration was put into effect for one week, but officials can extend it.
Neighboring Pasco and Pinellas counties have also declared similar states of emergency in relation to dengue reports.
The Florida department of health said in its recent report on mosquito-transmitted viruses that there were 26 cases of international travel-linked dengue reported in the state during a six-day period beginning on 13 September. There have been a total of 212 known travel-related cases in Florida reported so far in 2026.
Over the same period, there were 38 locally contracted dengue cases reported in Florida. They were among 190 cases of locally acquired dengue across Florida, the state’s health department said .
Numbers from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) differ slightly. As of Monday, the CDC noted 392 cases of dengue had been reported overall in Florida for the year so far, along with different county-level data.
Dengue is contracted through the bite of some mosquito species, largely Aedes aegypti , as well as Aedes albopictus . Both species are present in Florida.
Symptoms show up between three days and two weeks after a bite from an infected mosquito. Among the symptoms are “sudden onset of fever, severe headache, eye pain, muscle and joint pain … and bleeding. Gastrointestinal symptoms like vomiting and diarrhea may also be present in some cases,” Florida’s state health department said.
The symptoms typically span four days to one week. A rarer form of the illness called dengue hemorrhagic fever can be fatal without the administration of proper supportive care, the state health department said.
Hillsborough county authorities have expressed optimism that dengue infections might slow down in the coming weeks, with zero “mosquito test pools” testing positive recently, according to the local Bay News 9 outlet.

articles.title_orig: Young GeoPioneers launches in Columbia to teach kids about their world
articles.title_zh: Young GeoPioneers launches in Columbia to teach kids about their world
articles.content_orig:
Young GeoPioneers, which launched in Columbia on Saturday, seeks to teach kids about maps, satellites and geography to better understand their world.
COLUMBIA — Young GeoPioneers held its first free pilot event Saturday at Stephens Lake Park to teach children how to better understand the world.
The group is for ages 4 to 10 and focuses on using maps, Geographic Information Systems and satellite data to assess natural resources, the environment, the climate and the planet.
Young GeoPioneers founder Akanksha Balha said while kids are still young, this is the time to teach them answers to real-life questions.
"For example, anything about the environment, like how did the flood happen?" Balha said. "Or where did the flood water go, (or) where a hospital or a park should be located within a city so that it is good for the environment of the surroundings of the city?"
Balha has a doctorate in the application of remote sensing and GIS in urban areas and hydrology, and has been in the research field for 10 years. She said that teaching has always been a part of her work, and she loves teaching kids.
"This was a time when I felt like I want to start something of my own," Balha said. "Where I can teach kids and transfer what I know in this field to them."
Balha cited two main reasons for starting the group. She said geospatial technology is a big part of people's daily lives, and young people should be educated about it because they are the future.
The birds eye view photos Blaha used at Stephens lake park to demonstrate how satellites use visuals over land.

"I do not want them to know about it at a later stage when they go to high school or college, but now, earlier, as they are the future generation of ours and we are in such a technology-driven world," Balha said.
She also attributes starting the organization to her curious 17-month-old daughter. When she teaches her daughter about these topics, Balha feels like she pays very close attention.
Balha said she teaches the kids in an understandable and interactive way. On Saturday, the kid's activities were tailored to learn more about geoinformatics, which Balha said consists of remote sensing, satellite data and aerial imagery.
To make this understandable to kids, Balha said she printed out different bird's-eye view photos, and had the children act like birds and imagine how the bird would rise up and tilt to see the specific view.
"When it goes higher up, then how the surface will change in the dimensions, which they pick up like very easily," Balha said. "It was very interesting and easier for them to understand how things change, how the details of the dimensions change when (the) camera moves at a higher elevation, be it for a drone or a satellite."
She also had them read maps for a treasure hunt. Two groups were given a satellite photo of Stephens Lake marked with where the treasure was hidden and they had to use the map to find it.
Balha said she is currently in talks with the Daniel Boone Regional Library to start doing sessions, and she plans to start a paid pilot session at The Children's School at Stephens College.
For more information, visit Young GeoPioneers' Facebook page and Instagram . The group is working on getting a website live in the coming weeks at younggeopioneersllc.com .

articles.title_orig: What to know about Brazil’s 2026 presidential election
articles.title_zh: What to know about Brazil’s 2026 presidential election
articles.content_orig:
For the second election in a row, Brazilian voters face a choice between left-wing candidate Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and a right-wing candidate from the Bolsonaro family .
The country’s fractious election is set to take place during a wave of successful far-right candidates across Latin America and a sensitive time in Brazil’s modern political history.
Former right-wing President Jair Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year prison sentence over his role in a coup plot following his loss to Lula in 2022. The conviction of Jair Bolsonaro and several military officers raised questions about the resilience of Brazilian democracy, revived several decades ago following a period of rule by a United States-backed military dictatorship.
An explosive corruption scandal has implicated prominent figures and institutions across the political spectrum, and observers have expressed concern about possible US intervention .
Polls suggest Lula, the current president seeking a fourth non-consecutive term, and Bolsonaro’s eldest son, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, are in a virtual tie in a simulated run-off.
Who are the candidates, what issues have been front and centre, and what could the election mean for Brazil? Here’s what you need to know about Brazil’s 2026 presidential elections.
The first round of voting in the Brazilian presidential election will take place on October 4 from 8am to 5pm Brasilia time (11:00 to 20:00 GMT).
If no candidate wins the first round outright, the top two candidates will proceed to a run-off vote on October 25.
Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva , better known simply as Lula, is the country’s current president and the candidate for the Workers’ Party, or the PT.
The 80-year-old has been a central figure in Brazilian politics for decades, serving two four-year presidential terms between 2003 and 2011, and his current term, which began in 2023.
His time in office has been defined by an effort to pair political democracy, restored after a US-backed military dictatorship that ruled the country for several decades until the 1980s, with material improvement for the country’s poor through a series of social programmes meant to address inequality.
Lula has also sought to forge ties between developing, non-Western countries on the global stage .
“He has come to embody the institutionalisation and consolidation of Brazilian democracy since the end of the dictatorship,” Andre Pagliarini, an assistant professor of history and international studies at Louisiana State University and the author of a book on Lula, told Al Jazeera in a phone call.
Flavio Bolsonaro has emerged as the heir to his father’s status as leader of Brazil’s political right and Lula’s main challenger in the 2026 election. Bolsonaro is running as the candidate of the right-wing Liberal Party.
The 45-year-old is the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro.
Flavio has pledged a hard stance on crime and insecurity and close collaboration with the administration of US President Donald Trump, which has designated several criminal groups in Brazil as “terrorist organisations”.
He has also promised to rein in inflation and government spending, with an adviser stating that he would implement a debt ceiling if elected.
Flavio Bolsonaro has also sought to turn his father’s conviction into a story of political persecution, denouncing his trial as illegitimate and seeking his release from prison.
“I ask God for the opportunity to walk up the ramp of Planalto Palace next year alongside President Jair Messias Bolsonaro, so that he may place the presidential sash across my chest,” he said at a campaign event in September.
“The Bolsonaro family’s pitch is that the institutions that Brazilian democracy has erected since the end of dictatorship are either rotten and unresponsive, and that we need a sharp turn away from this status quo,” said Pagliarini.
“The stakes of this election are incredibly stark because the candidates stand for such opposing visions about what Brazil’s recent history means,” he added.
As with many recent elections across the region, crime, insecurity and cost of living issues have dominated the Brazilian election. Corruption and concerns about US intervention in the country’s domestic affairs have also loomed over the campaign.
A Quaest survey from September 7 found that 31 percent of respondents cited violence as their biggest concern, followed by 20 percent who said corruption, 19 percent who said the economy, and 12 percent who said health.
While Brazil has seen decent economic growth and low unemployment and inflation during Lula’s third term, those mild gains have been paired with explosive levels of household debt and concerns about the rising cost of living.
A report from the Center for Economic and Policy Research, a left-leaning US-based think tank focused on economic issues, found that extreme poverty in Brazil fell by about 40 percent between 2022 and 2024, unemployment dropped to historic lows, and the country’s economic growth significantly outpaced that of most of its neighbours. But the analysis also found that households were strained by a sharp uptick in the cost of servicing debt. All in all, analysts say they amount to a view of the economy that is neither catastrophic nor particularly satisfying.
Pagliarini says that both candidates have tried to steer the election onto more favourable terrain for their issues of choice, with Lula portraying Flavio Bolsonaro as a willing accomplice in US efforts to undermine Brazilian sovereignty, and Flavio Bolsonaro accusing Lula of being corrupt and weak on crime.
Analysts say that polls reflect the state of Brazilian politics: deeply polarised but unenthusiastic.
“The general vibe is that this is a very downbeat campaign,” said Pagliarini. “There’s not a lot of enthusiasm either way, and it’s hard to tell at this stage who that favours.”
Most surveys show a close race, with Lula holding a marginal advantage over Flavio Bolsonaro that tightens further in a hypothetical run-off.
A Quaest survey from September shows Lula with 37 percent of voter intention against Flavio Bolsonaro’s 33 percent, while an AtlasIntel survey from the same period showed Lula winning 46 percent to Flavio Bolsonaro’s 43 percent.
A Datafolha poll found Lula with 40 percent and Flavio Bolsonaro with 36 percent.
Polls also show Flavio Bolsonaro favoured over Lula on issues of inflation, combating corruption, and crime and drug trafficking, while Lula is seen more favourably on issues of poverty and inequality, foreign affairs and health.
An explosive corruption scandal, focused on disgraced banker Daniel Vorcaro, has raised questions for both campaigns and implicated members of the country’s political and economic elite across the political spectrum.
Reports found that Flavio Bolsonaro had solicited substantial funds from Vorcaro, ostensibly to finance a documentary – The Dark Horse (or O Azarao) – about his father.
Lula’s former finance minister, Guido Mantega, has also said he helped arrange a meeting with Vorcaro, Lula and the head of Brazil’s central bank to discuss banking policy. Lula has said he told Vorcaro there would be no political interference in his bank’s case, only a “technical investigation conducted by the central bank”. The Reuters news agency confirmed the meeting.
The scandal has also embroiled the country’s Supreme Court , with Alexandre de Moraes, whose central role in Bolsonaro’s coup trial turned him into a subject of ire for the political right, facing questions about his own links to the banker.
De Moraes has in turn accused a justice appointed by Bolsonaro of wrongdoing, with the court considering probes into the conduct of both justices.
Concerns that the Trump administration could intervene or seek to influence the outcome on behalf of Bolsonaro have also loomed over the election.

articles.title_orig: Paris police chief says student protest movement out of control, urges peaceful action
articles.title_zh: Paris police chief says student protest movement out of control, urges peaceful action
articles.content_orig:
Hundreds of schools were closed across France on Friday, after a swathe of student protests turned violent.
More than 400 schools were shut in the aftermath of the rallies, which saw thousands of students mobilize to voice their discontent with run-down school buildings, long days and teacher shortages.
French high school days can stretch from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m., depending on timetables.
The country's Interior Ministry reportedly said 1,027 of France's roughly 3,700 lycées, or high schools, were affected Thursday, including 222 that were blockaded.
The rallies turned increasingly violent this week, with some protesters clashing with police and setting fire to schools and vehicles. Dozens of educational staff, hundreds of police officers and more than 100 pupils are said to have been injured since the protests began, according to the French press.
Protests were held across the country as the movement, which began in Paris, spread nationwide.
Although Education Minister Édouard Geffray said in an interview that the movement was "legitimate at the outset," France's Interior Ministry said Thursday the unrest "no longer has anything to do with the legitimate expression of high-school students' demands."
The ministry described the situation as having the characteristics of "urban violence," according to French newspaper Le Monde.
Geffray is scheduled to meet with teachers' unions, student representatives and parents' groups on Friday.
The unrest is adding to a major political headache for the government, which is about to start tough budget negotiations against a backdrop of division and economic turmoil.
Officials presented a draft budget on Thursday, and the government is now tasked with convincing lawmakers in the politically fractured National Assembly to agree to the plans.
Following a crisis meeting, the Prime Minister's Office said intelligence services viewed the movement as a "maneuver organized by LFI and its ultra-left proxies," according to Reuters.
Some members of the left-wing La France Insoumise (LFI) party have publicly backed the student protests.
CNBC reached out to the LFI party and the Prime Minister's Office for comment.
Finance Minister Roland Lescure told reporters on Thursday that the 2027 budget was targeting a fiscal adjustment worth 54 billion euros ($60.8 billion). Cuts are planned to come, in part, from freezing wages for public sector workers like teachers.
The European Union's second-largest economy has repeatedly broken the bloc's rules on budget deficits and debt limits. Successive prime ministers have been ousted after failed attempts at reform, spending cuts and tax rises to bring the situation under control.
But with France under the EU's excessive deficit procedure and the government seeking tens of billions of euros in fiscal consolidation, demands for greater education spending come at a difficult time for the public finances.
EU treaties set reference values of 3% of GDP for government deficits and 60% for government debt. Last year, France's deficit reached 5.1% of GDP, while its debt-to-GDP ratio hit 119% by the end of June.
Concerns over France's huge debt pile and budget deficit — and political divisions presenting an obstacle to reducing both — have soured investor sentiment the country this year, with bond markets demanding increasing premiums to lend to the government.
Yields on French government bonds are now trading near multi-decade highs, with government borrowing costs now among the highest in the G7 group of advanced economies.
The yield on France's benchmark 10-year OAT was trading at 4.914% – 139 basis points higher than where it was 12 months ago and close to a 24-year high.
